blocks.p: The early 1990s saw a spate of bulk carrier losses, and their character is what made them so serious. These were not slow foundering casualties. Ships were being lost suddenly, often without a distress message and frequently with the whole crew, in weather that similar ships had survived for years. A ship that sinks in minutes gives nobody time to launch a boat, which is why the response had to be about preventing the flooding rather than improving the escape.

No figure is given here for ships or lives lost. IMO's own material describes the losses without quantifying them, published figures differ substantially, and an unverifiable number is better omitted than guessed.

blocks.h: 2. The primary mechanism - side shell to flooded hold

blocks.p: The dominant failure chain was understood to run like this, and it explains the suddenness:

ul: The ships were mostly single-side-skin designs, in which the side shell frames and their end brackets are directly exposed in the cargo hold.

Those frames corrode and fatigue faster than anything else on the ship. They alternate between wet and dry service, they are abraded by grabs and bulldozers during discharge, and coating breaks down first at the bracket toes where the stress concentration also is.
The foremost hold is the worst place for this. It takes the heaviest slamming and the greatest wave impact, and it is the least accessible for inspection.
A frame failure lets the side shell go, and No.1 hold floods.
The flooded hold now loads the transverse watertight bulkhead between holds 1 and 2 with a head of water it was never designed to hold. If that bulkhead fails, two holds flood.
With two forward holds full of water and dense cargo, the ship loses bow buoyancy and longitudinal strength together and goes down by the head, very quickly.

blocks.h: 3. The secondary mechanism - hatch covers and progressive flooding

ul: Water ingress through hatch covers and other openings is the other entry route IMO identifies - covers of inadequate strength, worn securing arrangements, or damaged coamings, in a seaway that puts green water on the foredeck.

Alternate-hold loading made it worse. Loading heavy cargo in alternate holds concentrates weight and raises local stresses, and once a hold is flooded the sloshing mixture of cargo and water attacks the boundaries and drives progressive flooding into the next space.
An ageing fleet. Many of the ships were built in the boom of the late 1960s and 1970s and were reaching the age at which accumulated wastage matters.

High-tensile steel. HTS gives the same strength in a thinner plate - which means the same percentage of corrosion removes a larger proportion of the remaining margin, and fatigue performance is not improved in proportion to yield strength.
Dense cargoes. Iron ore and similar cargoes fill only part of the hold volume but load the structure heavily, and they are discharged by mechanical means that damage the very frames that matter.
Maintenance and inspection. Coatings in cargo holds were often not maintained, and nothing obliged anyone to look closely at side shell frames within arm's reach on a routine basis.
Commercial pressure. Fast turnarounds, aggressive discharge and thin margins on old tonnage all worked against condition.

blocks.h: 5. IMO's response - what chapter XII is

blocks.p: SOLAS chapter XII - Additional safety measures for bulk carriers - was adopted in November 1997 and entered into force on 1 July 1999, with a further significant package of amendments in 2004. It was one of the first and most consequential products of the Formal Safety Assessment methodology: IMO ran FSA studies on bulk carrier safety following the re-opened investigation into the loss of the Derbyshire, and MSC 76, in December 2002, approved the resulting package including chapter XII and regulation XII/12.
The chapter attacks the failure chain in section 2 at every link, which is why it works and is the structure this answer follows.

ul: Survive the flooded hold. New bulk carriers of 150 m and above carrying solid bulk cargoes of density 1,000 kg/m3 and above must be able to withstand flooding of any one cargo hold, taking into account dynamic effects. This is the single most important provision: it breaks the chain at the point where one flooded hold became two.

Strengthen what failed. Requirements for the structural strength of bulk carriers - in particular the transverse watertight bulkhead and the double bottom in the flooded condition, and the side structure itself - gave statutory force to the classification-society work of the same period on frame scantlings and corrosion margins.

Protect the steel. Regulation XII/6 is the bulk carrier limb of the mandatory Performance Standard for Protective Coatings (resolution MSC.215(82)). Coating breakdown is the leading indicator of exactly the wastage that caused these losses.
Offer a better hull form. The 2004 amendments introduced double-side-skin construction as an alternative - which removes the exposed side shell frame from the cargo hold altogether.
Restrict the dangerous loading. The same package added restrictions on sailing with any hold empty for the ships and conditions most at risk.

Know that the hold is flooding. Regulation XII/12, effective 1 July 2004, requires water level detectors with alarms in cargo holds, ballast tanks and dry spaces - at 0.5 m above the inner bottom, and a second at not less than 15 per cent of hold depth but not more than 2.0 m. Crews had been losing ships without knowing a hold was full. This is the cheapest provision in the chapter and arguably the one that saves most lives.

Be able to do something about it. Regulation XII/13 requires that the means for draining and pumping dry space bilges and ballast tanks be operable from a readily accessible enclosed space - because the alarm is useless if reaching the valves means going forward on a flooded deck.

Load it correctly. Regulation XII/11 requires an approved loading instrument on bulk carriers of 150 m in length and upwards, so shear force and bending moment are monitored at every pour and every de-ballasting step. A cargo density declaration is required so that the ship is loaded on the right assumptions.

Look at it properly. Chapter XII carries survey and maintenance requirements and requires information on compliance to be carried aboard; these run together with SOLAS XI-1/2 and the 2011 ESP Code, under which close-up survey of the side shell frames within arm's reach and thickness measurement by an approved firm became a planned, mandatory programme rather than a matter of judgement.

blocks.h: 8. The contribution argued, and its limits

blocks.p: The contribution is best stated as defence in depth against one specific chain of events, and that is what makes chapter XII a good regulatory answer rather than merely a strict one:

ul: Prevent the frame failure - coatings, scantlings, double-side skin.
Contain the flooding if it happens - bulkhead and double bottom strength in the flooded condition, and survival with any one hold flooded.
Detect it early - water level alarms.
Respond to it - remotely operable pumping and draining.
Verify continuously - loading instrument, cargo density declaration, enhanced survey.
Any single measure could be defeated; the point is that the chain now has to break in several places at once.

blocks.p: Its limits should be stated too. Chapter XII is largely prospective - the strongest structural and stability requirements attach to new ships and to defined size and density thresholds, so an older ship below the threshold is reached mainly by the detection, survey and operational provisions rather than by the design ones. It cannot compel good maintenance, only inspect for its absence. And it does not touch the commercial pressure - fast discharge with grabs and bulldozers, short port stays, thin margins on old tonnage - that produced the condition in the first place. What it did do was remove the possibility of a ship being lost because nobody was required to look, and that is the honest measure of its contribution.

Two tasks, and the examiner has weighted them for you: briefly discuss the reasons, then explain how chapter XII contributes. So keep the history tight - roughly a third - and spend the rest on the chapter. The best answers do one thing above all: they make the two halves match. Set out the failure chain first, then show chapter XII attacking it link by link. An answer that lists causes and then separately lists regulations has written two answers; an answer that says this provision exists because of that failure has written one.

blocks.h: The failure chain in one sentence

blocks.p: Learn it as a chain and the whole question unlocks: corroded and fatigued side shell frame -> side shell opens -> No.1 hold floods -> the transverse bulkhead sees a head of water it was never designed for -> two holds flood -> the bow loses buoyancy and the ship goes down by the head in minutes. Every element of chapter XII is a cut across one of those arrows, and you can derive the chapter from the chain if you forget the regulation numbers.

blocks.h: Why the FOREMOST hold, and why HIGH-TENSILE STEEL

blocks.p: Two details separate a competent answer from a good one. The foremost hold is where the ship takes the heaviest slamming and wave impact, where the structure is most highly stressed in a seaway, and where inspection access is worst - so the damage is greatest exactly where it is least likely to be seen. High-tensile steel is the subtler point and examiners like it: HTS delivers the same strength in a thinner plate, so the same rate of corrosion consumes a much larger proportion of the margin, and fatigue strength does not rise in proportion to yield strength. A design that is perfectly sound as built has less tolerance for the wastage that then occurs. This is also why the surveyor must know from the scantling drawings which plates are HTS - the same measured thickness can be acceptable in one plate and a rejection in another.

blocks.h: This paper asks the same question twice

blocks.p: Read this with Q5 of this same paper, on the Enhanced Survey Programme. The two are the same casualty record answered from opposite ends. Chapter XII is the construction and operational answer - survive the flooded hold, protect the coatings, detect the water, restrict the loading. The ESP is the inspection answer, which is exactly why Annex A of the ESP Code is the bulk carrier annex and why the regime concentrates on close-up survey of side shell frames and end brackets within arm's reach. In one sentence: the ships were lost through corrosion and fatigue of side structure that nobody was required to look at closely, and IMO responded by both strengthening the ship and mandating that somebody look. If you can write that sentence you can answer either question.

Chapter XII is one of the earliest and most consequential products of Formal Safety Assessment. IMO did not respond to these losses by tightening a rule at random; it ran structured FSA studies on bulk carrier safety after the re-opened investigation into the loss of the Derbyshire, and MSC 76 in December 2002 approved the resulting package. If a question on FSA ever asks you for a real example of the method producing regulation, this is the strongest one available - and it works the other way round too, because saying so here shows the examiner you know how the rule came to exist and not merely that it does.

ul: Quoting a number of ships or lives lost. The published figures differ substantially and IMO's own material does not quantify them - characterise the record instead.
Saying chapter XII made double-side-skin construction mandatory. It was introduced as an alternative.
Treating the losses as a stability problem. They were a structural problem whose consequence was a stability and buoyancy failure.
Listing regulations without connecting each to the failure it prevents. The stem says contribute towards the safety - that is a causal claim and must be argued.
Forgetting the detection provisions. The water level alarms are the cheapest measure in the chapter and probably the highest-value one.
Claiming chapter XII fixed everything. Its strongest structural provisions are largely prospective and threshold-limited, and it cannot compel good maintenance.

blocks.p:
"Why did the ships sink so fast?" Because the failure was structural and progressive: a flooded forward hold overloads the bulkhead behind it, and when that goes, two holds full of water and dense cargo take the bow down in minutes. That is also why there was often no distress message.

"What must a bulk carrier survive under chapter XII?" New ships of 150 m and above carrying cargoes of density 1,000 kg/m3 and above must withstand flooding of any one cargo hold, taking into account dynamic effects.

"Where are the water level alarms set?" 0.5 m above the inner bottom, and a second at not less than 15 per cent of hold depth but not more than 2.0 m - regulation XII/12.

"Which ships need a loading instrument?" Bulk carriers of 150 m in length and upwards, regulation XII/11.

"Why does the pumping requirement specify where you operate it from?" Because regulation XII/13 is useless otherwise - the alarm has just told you a forward hold is flooding, and that is precisely when nobody should be going forward on deck.

ul: When was chapter XII adopted and when did it come into force? Adopted November 1997; in force 1 July 1999.
What is the title of chapter XII? Additional safety measures for bulk carriers.
Which structural member was the primary culprit? The side shell frames and their end brackets in single-side-skin ships, especially in the foremost hold.
Why does high-tensile steel matter? Thinner plate for the same strength, so the same corrosion takes a larger proportion of the margin, and fatigue does not improve in proportion.
What does regulation XII/6 require? The bulk carrier limb of the mandatory Performance Standard for Protective Coatings, resolution MSC.215(82).
What did the 2004 amendments add? Restrictions on sailing with any hold empty, and double-side-skin construction as an alternative.

How does chapter XII relate to the ESP? Chapter XII strengthens and equips the ship; SOLAS XI-1/2 with the ESP Code makes somebody look at it closely, and Annex A of that Code is the bulk carrier annex.

blocks.p: CHAIN, then FIVE VERBS. The chain: frame - shell - hold - bulkhead - bow (steps 2 to 3). The five verbs are chapter XII: PREVENT (coatings XII/6, scantlings, double-side skin), CONTAIN (survive any one hold flooded, bulkhead and double bottom strength), DETECT (XII/12 alarms - 0.5 m, 15 per cent, 2.0 m), RESPOND (XII/13 pumping from an enclosed space), VERIFY (XII/11 loading instrument at 150 m, density declaration, enhanced survey). Dates: adopted 1997, in force 1 July 1999, alarms 1 July 2004.

THE CHAIN: single-side-skin ships have side shell frames and end brackets exposed in the hold; they corrode and fatigue fastest, being alternately wet and dry, abraded by grabs and bulldozers, with coating failing first at the bracket toes; the FOREMOST hold is worst because it takes the heaviest slamming and has the poorest access; a frame fails, the side shell opens, No.1 hold floods, the transverse watertight bulkhead behind it sees a head of water it was never designed for, TWO holds flood, and the bow goes down in minutes. Also: water ingress through HATCH COVERS, and alternate-hold loading concentrating stress and driving progressive flooding by sloshing cargo and water. WHY THEN: ageing fleet, HIGH-TENSILE STEEL giving thinner plate so the same corrosion eats a larger proportion of the margin, dense cargoes, unmaintained hold coatings, and no obligation to inspect side shell frames closely. THE ANSWER - SOLAS CHAPTER XII, Additional safety measures for bulk carriers, ADOPTED NOVEMBER 1997, IN FORCE 1 JULY 1999, further amendments 2004; one of the earliest products of FORMAL SAFETY ASSESSMENT, the package approved at MSC 76 in December 2002. questions.understand_first: These ships were not lost because they were badly loaded or badly handled. They were lost because a structural member nobody was required to look at closely failed, and because the ship had no defence once it had. That is the whole question, and it explains the shape of the answer: a chain of events, and a chapter of regulations written to cut the chain in as many places as possible. Hold the chain - frame, shell, hold, bulkhead, bow - and you can derive most of chapter XII from first principles even if the regulation numbers escape you. It also explains why the response came in two parts that this same examination paper asks about separately: strengthen and equip the ship, which is chapter XII, and make somebody look at it, which is the enhanced survey regime.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Describe the failure chain that sank these ships.
retrieval_cards.answer: A side shell frame or end bracket in a single-side-skin ship, corroded and fatigued by alternately wet and dry service and by grab and bulldozer abrasion, fails - most likely in the foremost hold, which takes the heaviest slamming and has the poorest inspection access. The side shell opens and No.1 hold floods. The transverse watertight bulkhead between holds 1 and 2 is then loaded with a head of water it was never designed to withstand; if it fails, two holds flood, and the ship loses bow buoyancy and longitudinal strength together and goes down by the head in minutes.
retrieval_cards.why: The suddenness is the point - it is why there was often no distress message and no time to launch a boat.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What flooded-hold survival requirement does chapter XII impose, and on which ships?
retrieval_cards.answer: New bulk carriers of 150 m in length and above, carrying solid bulk cargoes of density 1,000 kg/m3 and above, must be able to withstand flooding of any one cargo hold, taking into account dynamic effects. It is the provision that breaks the chain at the point where one flooded hold became two.
retrieval_cards.why: Both thresholds are examinable and the phrase 'taking into account dynamic effects' is the part candidates drop.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does SOLAS XII/12 require, and at what levels?
retrieval_cards.answer: Water level detectors with audible and visual alarms in cargo holds, ballast tanks and dry spaces. Alarms at 0.5 m above the inner bottom, and a second at not less than 15 per cent of the depth of the hold but not more than 2.0 m. Effective 1 July 2004.
retrieval_cards.why: Crews had been losing ships without knowing a hold was full. Cheapest provision in the chapter, arguably the highest value.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When was chapter XII adopted and brought into force, and what is it called?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS chapter XII, Additional safety measures for bulk carriers. Adopted November 1997 and entered into force on 1 July 1999, with a further significant amendment package in 2004 adding restrictions on sailing with any hold empty and double-side-skin construction as an alternative.
retrieval_cards.why: Adoption and entry into force are different dates and both are asked for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does high-tensile steel make the corrosion problem worse?
retrieval_cards.answer: HTS provides the same strength in a thinner plate, so a given rate of corrosion removes a much larger proportion of the material that was there - the absolute corrosion margin is smaller. Fatigue strength also does not increase in proportion to yield strength. A structure that is entirely sound as built therefore has less tolerance for the wastage that then occurs, which is also why the surveyor must know from the scantling drawings which plates are HTS before judging a thickness measurement.
retrieval_cards.why: The subtler of the two mechanism points, and the one that separates a good answer from a competent one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Did chapter XII make double-side-skin construction mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The 2004 amendments introduced double-side-skin construction as an ALTERNATIVE to the strengthened single-side-skin requirements. Its safety value is that it removes the exposed side shell frame from the cargo hold altogether, which is where the failure chain began.
retrieval_cards.why: Reversing the mandatory/alternative distinction is a marked error, and the reason double-side skin helps is worth a sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Summarise how chapter XII contributes, in five verbs.
retrieval_cards.answer: PREVENT - protective coatings under XII/6 and MSC.215(82), stronger scantlings, double-side skin. CONTAIN - survival with any one hold flooded, and bulkhead and double bottom strength in the flooded condition. DETECT - XII/12 water level alarms. RESPOND - XII/13 draining and pumping operable from a readily accessible enclosed space. VERIFY - XII/11 loading instrument, cargo density declaration, and enhanced survey under SOLAS XI-1/2 with the ESP Code. The chain now has to break in several places at once.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem's word 'contribute' is a causal claim; defence in depth is how you argue it rather than list it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does chapter XII NOT reach?
retrieval_cards.answer: Its strongest structural and stability requirements are largely prospective and threshold-limited, so an older or smaller ship is reached mainly by the detection, survey and operational provisions rather than by the design ones. It cannot compel good maintenance, only inspect for its absence. And it does not touch the commercial pressure - fast mechanical discharge, short port stays, thin margins on old tonnage - that produced the condition. What it did remove was the possibility of a ship being lost because nobody was required to look.
retrieval_cards.why: An 'explain how it contributes' answer that claims the problem is solved has overstated it; the honest limit is worth marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How did chapter XII come to exist, and why is that worth saying?
retrieval_cards.answer: Through Formal Safety Assessment. IMO ran structured FSA studies on bulk carrier safety following the re-opened investigation into the loss of the Derbyshire, and MSC 76 in December 2002 approved the resulting package, including chapter XII and regulation XII/12. It is one of the earliest and most consequential products of the method.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows you know how the rule came to exist and not merely that it does - and it is the strongest real example available if an FSA question ever asks for one.

blocks.h: 1. The propeller curve and the load diagram

blocks.p: A fixed pitch propeller absorbs power according to the propeller law: for a given hull condition, power varies roughly as the cube of the revolutions and torque roughly as the square. Plotted as power against rpm, that gives the propeller curve. The engine builder plots the engine's own limits on the same axes as the engine layout and load diagram, and the ship is designed so that the propeller curve sits comfortably inside them.

In MAN Energy Solutions' presentation of the load diagram, line 6 is the light propeller curve - for a clean hull and calm weather. That is the reference condition, and it is deliberately not where the engine is laid out.

Torque rich - the term the examiner uses - is what the engine builder calls heavy running. The propeller is absorbing more torque at a given speed of rotation than the light propeller curve predicts. Equivalently, and this is the more useful way to say it:

ul: for the same power, the engine runs at lower rpm than it should;
for the same rpm, the engine must develop more torque, which means more fuel per cycle and higher mean effective pressure;
the operating point moves up and to the left on the load diagram, away from the light propeller curve and towards the torque limit.

blocks.p: That last movement is the whole problem, because of what the limit is. Line 4 of the load diagram is the torque/speed limit of the engine, and it is limited mainly by the THERMAL LOAD on the engine. Note also that line 5, the maximum mean effective pressure for continuous operation, is a limit only at high loads and speeds - at lower speeds line 4 is the stricter limit, which is precisely the region a heavy-running ship is driven into. A torque rich engine is therefore not merely inefficient; it is being pushed toward a limit that exists to protect it from thermal overload.

blocks.h: 3. Why the light running margin exists

blocks.p: Because heavy running is expected, the engine is deliberately laid out to the right of the light propeller curve. The gap is the light running margin:
LRM = (nL - nH) / nH x 100 per cent, where nL is the light propeller curve speed and nH the heavier engine layout curve speed.

MAN Energy Solutions recommends a light running margin of 4 to 7 per cent, depending on the specific ship and operational profile, and up to 10 per cent in special cases. It sits alongside the sea margin - typically 10 to 30 per cent, historically 15 per cent - and the engine margin, historically 10 per cent and typically 10 to 30 per cent. So a new ship on trials is light running by design. Torque rich means the ship has consumed that designed-in margin and gone past it.

A single figure gives the sensitivity, and it is worth remembering: a 20 per cent increase in required power from added resistance corresponds to about 1 per cent heavy running - one per cent lower rpm for the same engine power. The rpm shift is small and the power penalty behind it is very large, which is exactly why the condition is missed.
Anything that increases the resistance of the ship, or the load on the propeller, at a given speed of rotation.

ul: Hull fouling. The first and commonest cause. Frictional resistance increases with fouling of the hull by the growth of algae, sea grass and barnacles, and frictional resistance is the dominant component for most merchant hull forms at service speed. Long idle periods in warm water are the classic history.

Propeller fouling and roughness. A fouled, pitted or damaged blade surface degrades efficiency directly, and the propeller is a far smaller area than the hull - so a given amount of roughness there matters disproportionately.
Propeller damage. A bent, eroded or broken blade tip changes the absorbed torque and adds vibration.
Weather and sea state. Wind, waves and swell, particularly on the bow. This is the condition the sea margin exists for; heavy weather simply uses it up.

Shallow water. In general there is no influence when the water depth is more than ten times the ship's draught. Below that the resistance can rise significantly - the pressure field around the hull is intensified and the wave system enlarged, water flows back around the restricted section, and the propeller draws water past the hull faster than in deep water.
Adverse current, and restricted or confined water. Canals and narrow channels combine shallow-water and bank effects.
Displacement and trim. A deeper draught than the design condition, or a trim away from the optimum, increases resistance.

Towing, pushing, or an ice-bound passage, and in the limit the bollard pull condition, which is heavy running taken to its extreme: a heavy running factor of 15 to 20 per cent relative to the light propeller curve has been experienced there - equivalent to roughly a 60 to 100 per cent increase in power for the same rpm, which is why full rpm simply cannot be reached at bollard pull.
An over-pitched or wrongly matched propeller, or a propeller repaired to the wrong pitch. Here the ship is heavy running from new or from the repair, not through fouling.
On a controllable pitch propeller, excessive pitch demand for the rpm - a mis-set or drifting combinator curve, or a fault in the pitch control or feedback.
Hull deformation or appendage damage, and a damaged or permanently offset rudder.

blocks.p: Separate what the engine tells you from what the ship tells you, because the diagnosis needs both.

ul: The defining indication: rpm and fuel index disagree with the reference condition. At a given rpm the fuel pump index is higher than the shop and sea trial data, or the sea trial curve, would give - the engine is working harder for the revolutions it is making.
Rated rpm cannot be reached at full load. The engine comes up against its limit before it reaches its speed.
Higher exhaust gas temperatures and rising thermal load, since more fuel is being burnt per cycle at a lower air throughput.

Scavenge air pressure is low for the fuel being burnt. Turbocharger speed follows exhaust energy and engine rpm, so at reduced rpm the air supply lags the fuel demand - the air-fuel ratio falls, combustion deteriorates, and black smoke appears.
Higher mean effective pressure and altered indicator diagram - compression and maximum pressures shifting relative to the reference set.
Turbocharger surging in a severe case, and higher exhaust deposit and fouling rates over time.

The engine's own protection acting - the governor at the index limit, or the scavenge air pressure or torque limiter cutting back the fuel, is the control system telling you the operating point has reached line 4.
Speed loss. Lower speed over the ground and through the water for the same power, once current and weather are allowed for.
Fuel consumption per mile rises for the same passage and condition.

Performance monitoring trends. Plotted against the reference curve, the ship's operating points drift steadily to the left over weeks and months - which is what distinguishes fouling from a single weather event.
On the load diagram itself, the plotted operating point sits above the light propeller curve and approaches line 4.

blocks.p: The instruction to the second engineer begins here, and it matters, because acting on a faulty sensor wastes a hull cleaning.

ul: Take a full set of engine performance readings - indicator or pressure-rise diagrams, fuel index, rpm, scavenge air pressure and temperature, exhaust temperatures, turbocharger speed - and compare them against the shop and sea trial reference data for the same condition.

Verify the instruments before believing them. Tachometer, shaft power meter or torsionmeter, thermocouples, pressure gauges and the fuel index scale. A drifting torsionmeter has sent ships to dry dock unnecessarily.

Correct for the obvious. Draught, trim and displacement, weather, current and water depth. If the ship is in ten metres of water at deep draught she is heavy running for a reason that will disappear at the next sea buoy.

Exclude engine-side causes that mimic heavy running: fouled turbocharger or air cooler, high air cooler differential pressure, blocked scavenge ports or exhaust gas boiler, incorrect injection timing or VIT setting, leaking exhaust valves, and poor fuel quality, viscosity or calorific value. These reduce available power at rpm and look similar on the instruments, but the cure is entirely different.
Bring the operating point back inside the diagram - reduce the fuel index and accept the lower rpm. Do not chase the revolutions with more fuel; that is what drives the engine into the torque limit.

Do not run in the overload area other than as the maker permits - overload running is allowed only for limited periods, one hour per twelve hours, or when required in an emergency, because the thermal load is high.
Confirm the limiters are working - scavenge air pressure limiter, torque limiter, load programme - rather than defeating them.

Increase surveillance while the condition persists: exhaust temperature deviation between units, liner wall temperatures, scavenge space inspection for signs of poor combustion, and turbocharger condition.

blocks.h: 9. Remedy, report, and where authority stops

ul: Propeller polishing first. It is the cheapest and quickest intervention, it can be done by divers in many ports, and the gain per square metre cleaned is the highest on the ship.
Underwater hull cleaning, subject to the port's rules on in-water cleaning and biofouling discharge, and hull cleaning and recoating at the next dry docking.
Underwater inspection of the propeller for damage, erosion and blade deformation, and of the rudder and appendages.
On a CPP, check and calibrate the pitch setting, feedback and combinator curve, and confirm that the demanded pitch at each rpm is what the maker intended.
Optimise trim and ballast for the loaded condition where the ship's trim guidance allows it.
Log and trend everything, so the case rests on data rather than impression, and feed it into the ship's performance monitoring.
Report to the Chief Engineer, who informs the master and the Company. Speed and consumption are charter-party matters and the shore organisation must know.

Escalate the diagnosis, do not decide it. If the ship remains heavy running with a clean hull and a sound propeller, the fault is a matching problem, and the remedy - re-pitching, de-pitching or replacing the propeller, or a re-rating - is an owner's decision taken with the propeller designer, the engine builder and class. The second engineer establishes and preserves the evidence; he does not prescribe the cure.

Consult the ship's own documentation throughout. The light running margin actually built into your vessel is in her project papers and her engine load diagram - not in any general figure, including the ones quoted above.

blocks.p: Four printed limbs and the marks are evenly spread, so answer all four visibly and head each one. The examiner has told you where to start: "Referring to propeller Curve". That is not scene-setting, it is the instruction - the definition in limb (a) is only precise relative to the propeller curve, and an answer that says 'the engine is overloaded' without drawing or describing the curve has not defined anything. Sketch the load diagram if you can: light propeller curve, engine layout curve, the torque limit, and the operating point sitting between them. Everything in limbs (b), (c) and (d) can then be pointed at on the diagram, which is far faster to write than to describe in prose.

The Indian examination uses torque rich; the engine builders' documentation says heavy running. They are the same condition, and knowing both names is worth a line in the answer, because every maker's manual, load diagram and service letter you will ever consult uses the second one. The complementary term is light running - which is not a fault but the designed condition: a new ship on trials with a clean hull runs light on purpose, and the deliberate gap is the light running margin.

blocks.h: The one number that explains why it is missed

blocks.p: MAN's rule of thumb: a 20 per cent increase in required power from added resistance corresponds to about 1 per cent heavy running - one per cent lower rpm for the same power. Read that twice. The rpm change is tiny and the power penalty behind it is enormous. A watchkeeper glancing at a tachometer will never see it; only comparison with the reference condition will. That single relationship is the argument for systematic performance monitoring, and quoting it in limb (c) shows you understand why the indications have to be compared rather than merely read.

blocks.h: Why the torque limit is where it is

blocks.p: Line 4 of the load diagram is the torque/speed limit, and it is limited mainly by the THERMAL load on the engine. That is the sentence to remember, because it explains why torque rich is dangerous rather than merely uneconomic. At reduced rpm the turbocharger turns more slowly and delivers less air, while the fuel demanded per cycle has gone up - so the air-fuel ratio falls exactly when more heat is being released. Higher exhaust temperatures, black smoke, fouling and thermal stress all follow from that one imbalance. Note too that line 5, the mep limit, bites only at high loads and speeds; at lower speeds line 4 is the stricter limit, which is precisely the corner a heavy-running ship is pushed into.

blocks.h: The trap in limb (d): confirm before you clean

blocks.p: The instinctive answer to limb (d) is 'clean the hull and polish the propeller'. That is the right ending and the wrong beginning, and examiners notice. Several engine-side faults imitate heavy running on the instruments - a fouled turbocharger or air cooler, incorrect injection timing or VIT, leaking exhaust valves, poor fuel quality - and so does a drifting torsionmeter or tachometer. All of them reduce the power available at a given rpm and all of them look similar. The disciplined sequence is confirm, exclude, protect, then remedy: verify against reference data, check the instruments, correct for draught, weather and water depth, exclude the engine side, reduce load to get off the torque limit, and only then arrange the diver. A candidate who sends the ship for an underwater clean because a thermocouple has drifted has answered the question badly even though the words look right.

ul: Defining torque rich without reference to the propeller curve, when the stem expressly says to refer to it.
Saying the engine is 'overloaded'. It is mismatched - operating off its design curve toward the torque limit. Overload is a different and defined region of the diagram.
Treating light running as a fault. It is the design intent, and the light running margin exists precisely so the ship can go heavy in service and still make her power.
Answering limb (d) with 'clean the hull' and nothing else - no confirmation, no instrument check, no engine-side exclusion, no immediate protection.
Chasing the rpm with more fuel. That is the single most damaging response, because it drives the engine straight into the thermal limit the diagram exists to keep it away from.
Quoting a fuel penalty percentage for fouling. Published values vary enormously with coating, trade, water temperature and lay-up; explain the mechanism instead.
Forgetting the CPP case, where a mis-set combinator curve produces the identical symptoms with a perfectly clean hull.

blocks.p:
"Your ship is 1 per cent down on rpm at the same power. Is that significant?" Yes - roughly a 20 per cent increase in required power. The smallness of the rpm figure is the trap.

"Why not just increase the fuel to get the revolutions back?" Because you would be driving the engine into line 4, the torque/speed limit, which is set by thermal load. You would be trading a fuel penalty for liner, piston and exhaust valve damage.

"How much overload running is permitted?" Only for limited periods - one hour per twelve hours, or when required in an emergency, because the thermal load is high.

"When does shallow water matter?" In general there is no influence when the depth is more than ten times the draught. Below that it can be significant.

"The hull was cleaned last month and she is still heavy. What now?" Suspect the propeller - damage, roughness, or wrong pitch after a repair - or, on a CPP, the pitch control. If the hull and propeller are both sound, it is a matching problem and it goes to the owner, the propeller designer, the engine builder and class. It is not a decision for the engine room.

ul: What is the propeller law? Power varies roughly as the cube of rpm and torque roughly as the square, for a given hull condition.

What is the light running margin, and what does the maker recommend? The rpm margin between the light propeller curve and the engine layout curve; MAN Energy Solutions recommends 4 to 7 per cent, and up to 10 per cent in special cases.
Which line on the load diagram is the torque limit, and what sets it? The torque/speed limit line, set mainly by the thermal load on the engine.

Name three causes of heavy running that have nothing to do with fouling. Heavy weather; shallow water; an over-pitched or damaged propeller. Add restricted water, deep draught, towing, and CPP pitch control faults.
What is the first indication you would look for? Fuel index higher than the reference value at the same rpm.
Why does black smoke appear? The turbocharger turns more slowly at reduced rpm and delivers less air, while fuel per cycle has increased - the air-fuel ratio falls.

How heavy is a propeller running at bollard pull? A heavy running factor of about 15 to 20 per cent relative to the light propeller curve, equivalent to roughly a 60 to 100 per cent power increase at the same rpm.
Whose decision is it to change the propeller pitch? The owner's, with the propeller designer, the engine builder and class - not the ship's.

blocks.p: CURVE - CAUSE - CLUE - CURE. Curve: propeller law, light propeller curve, layout curve, light running margin, and line 4 the torque limit set by thermal load (limb a). Cause: anything adding resistance or propeller load - fouling, weather, shallow water, draught and trim, damage, wrong pitch, CPP settings (limb b). Clue: index up at the same rpm, rated rpm unreachable, exhaust temperatures up, scavenge air low for the fuel, smoke, surging, speed and consumption adrift (limb c). Cure: confirm, exclude, protect, remedy, report - in that order (limb d). One number to carry: 20 per cent more power for 1 per cent fewer revolutions.

quick_revision.recall_15s: TORQUE RICH is what the engine builders call HEAVY RUNNING. Define it against the PROPELLER CURVE: for a given hull condition power varies roughly as the CUBE of rpm and torque as the SQUARE. Heavy running means the propeller absorbs MORE TORQUE AT A GIVEN RPM than the light propeller curve predicts - so for the same power the rpm is LOWER, for the same rpm the torque, fuel per cycle and mep are HIGHER, and the operating point moves UP AND LEFT on the load diagram toward the torque limit. That limit matters: LINE 4 IS THE TORQUE/SPEED LIMIT AND IT IS SET MAINLY BY THE THERMAL LOAD ON THE ENGINE, and while line 5 (mep) bites only at high load and speed, AT LOWER SPEEDS LINE 4 IS THE STRICTER LIMIT. Because heavy running is expected, the engine is laid out to the RIGHT of the light propeller curve - the LIGHT RUNNING MARGIN, LRM = (nL - nH)/nH x 100%, which MAN RECOMMENDS AT 4 TO 7%, up to 10% in special cases, alongside sea margin (typically 10-30%, historically 15%) and engine margin (historically 10%). KEY SENSITIVITY: a 20% INCREASE IN REQUIRED POWER CORRESPONDS TO ABOUT 1% HEAVY RUNNING - tiny rpm change, huge power penalty, which is why it is missed. REASONS: hull fouling by algae, sea grass and barnacles; propeller fouling, roughness or damage; heavy weather; SHALLOW WATER - no influence in general above TEN TIMES THE DRAUGHT; adverse current and restricted water; deep draught or bad trim; towing, pushing, ice; BOLLARD PULL as the extreme, 15-20% heavy running, equal to 60-100% more power for the same rpm; an over-pitched or wrongly repaired propeller; on a CPP a mis-set combinator curve or pitch feedback fault; hull or rudder damage. Confirm against shop and sea trial data; verify tachometer, torsionmeter and gauges; correct for draught, trim, weather and water depth; EXCLUDE engine-side mimics - fouled turbocharger or air cooler, injection timing or VIT, leaking exhaust valves, poor fuel. PROTECT: reduce fuel index and accept lower rpm, DO NOT CHASE RPM WITH FUEL; overload only as permitted, ONE HOUR IN TWELVE or in emergency; confirm limiters work. REMEDY: propeller polishing first, then underwater hull cleaning subject to port rules, propeller and rudder inspection, CPP pitch and combinator calibration, trim optimisation. REPORT: log and trend, report to the Chief Engineer who informs master and Company - and if hull and propeller are sound it is a MATCHING problem for the owner with the propeller designer, engine builder and class, not a decision for the engine room.

questions.understand_first: The engine and the propeller are matched to each other on one diagram, and everything in this question is a movement on that diagram. The propeller absorbs power as roughly the cube of its speed; the engine builder draws that curve alongside the engine's own limits and then deliberately lays the engine out a few per cent to the right of it, because he knows the hull will foul and the weather will be bad. That deliberate gap is the light running margin. Torque rich simply means the ship has used up that margin and gone past it - the propeller now demands more torque than the engine can give at that speed, so the operating point drifts toward the torque limit, which exists because of thermal load. Hold that picture and the rest is derivable: the causes are anything that adds resistance, the indications are departures from the reference condition rather than absolute readings, and the cure is to stop pushing, find what added the resistance, and take it away.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define torque rich with reference to the propeller curve.
retrieval_cards.answer: The propeller is absorbing more torque at a given speed of rotation than the light propeller curve predicts - the maker's term is heavy running. Equivalently: for the same power the engine runs at lower rpm; for the same rpm it must develop more torque, so more fuel per cycle and higher mean effective pressure; and the operating point moves up and to the left on the load diagram, away from the light propeller curve and toward the torque/speed limit.
retrieval_cards.why: Defining it as generic 'overload' loses the marks. It is a mismatch against a specific reference curve.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the light running margin, and what does the maker recommend?
retrieval_cards.answer: The rpm margin between the light propeller curve and the engine layout curve: LRM = (nL - nH) / nH x 100 per cent. MAN Energy Solutions recommends 4 to 7 per cent depending on the specific ship and operational profile, and up to 10 per cent in special cases. It sits alongside the sea margin - typically 10 to 30 per cent, historically 15 - and the engine margin, historically 10 per cent.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows that light running is the design intent, not a fault, and that torque rich means the designed margin has been consumed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How much extra power does 1 per cent heavy running represent?
retrieval_cards.answer: As a rule of thumb, a 20 per cent increase in required power from added resistance corresponds to about 1 per cent heavy running - that is, 1 per cent lower rpm for the same engine power.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most useful number in the topic: the rpm change is tiny and the power penalty behind it is enormous, which is exactly why the condition goes unnoticed without performance monitoring.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which limit does a torque rich engine approach, and what sets that limit?
retrieval_cards.answer: The torque/speed limit line of the engine load diagram - line 4 in MAN's numbering - which is limited mainly by the THERMAL load on the engine. The mean effective pressure limit is a constraint only at high loads and speeds; at lower speeds the torque/speed limit is the stricter one, which is precisely the region a heavy-running ship is driven into.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why torque rich is a damage risk and not merely a fuel-economy problem.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When does shallow water cause heavy running, and how heavy is bollard pull?
retrieval_cards.answer: In general shallow water has no influence when the water depth is more than ten times the ship's draught; below that it can increase resistance significantly. Bollard pull is the extreme case of heavy running: a heavy running factor of 15 to 20 per cent relative to the light propeller curve has been experienced, equivalent to roughly a 60 to 100 per cent increase in power for the same rpm - which is why full rpm cannot be reached at bollard pull.
retrieval_cards.why: Two checkable figures that show the reasons limb has been understood rather than listed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the defining indication of heavy running, and why is it a comparison rather than a reading?
retrieval_cards.answer: The fuel pump index is higher than the shop and sea trial reference value at the same rpm - the engine is working harder for the revolutions it is making. It must be a comparison because the absolute values mean nothing on their own: a 1 per cent rpm shift is invisible on a tachometer while representing about 20 per cent more power, so only comparison against the reference condition reveals it.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the argument for systematic performance monitoring, and it is what separates a diagnosis from an impression.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship appears torque rich. What do you tell the second engineer to do, in order?
retrieval_cards.answer: CONFIRM - take a full performance set and compare against shop and sea trial data. VERIFY the instruments: tachometer, torsionmeter or shaft power meter, thermocouples and gauges. CORRECT for draught, trim, weather, current and water depth. EXCLUDE engine-side causes that mimic it: fouled turbocharger or air cooler, injection timing and VIT, leaking exhaust valves, poor fuel quality. PROTECT: reduce the fuel index and accept the lower rpm, never chasing rpm with fuel, and keep out of the overload area beyond what the maker permits. REMEDY: propeller polishing first, then underwater hull cleaning subject to port rules, propeller and rudder inspection, CPP pitch and combinator calibration, trim optimisation. REPORT: log and trend, and report to the Chief Engineer, who informs the master and the Company.
retrieval_cards.why: The instinctive answer is 'clean the hull', which is the right ending and the wrong beginning - a drifting torsionmeter has sent ships to dry dock unnecessarily.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must you not simply increase fuel to recover the lost revolutions?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the engine is already being driven toward its torque/speed limit, which is set mainly by thermal load. More fuel at reduced rpm means more heat released while the turbocharger, turning more slowly, delivers less air - so the air-fuel ratio falls further. The result is higher exhaust temperatures, black smoke, fouling and thermal stress on liners, pistons and exhaust valves. You would be trading a fuel penalty for engine damage.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most damaging response available, and the one the load diagram exists to prevent.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The hull was cleaned and the propeller polished, and she is still heavy. What now, and whose decision is it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Suspect the propeller itself - damage, erosion, blade deformation, or the wrong pitch after a repair - and on a controllable pitch propeller the pitch setting, feedback and combinator curve. If hull and propeller are both sound, the ship has a MATCHING problem rather than a fouling problem. blocks.p: Ship health and vector control are governed by the International Health Regulations (2005), a binding instrument of the World Health Organization, as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024. The 2024 amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025. The IHR work through designated points of entry, competent authorities at those points, and a small set of ship documents.

ul: It makes the rules. WHO adopts the IHR and prescribes the model certificates in Annex 3 and the Ship Declaration of Health in Annex 8, so the documents are the same worldwide.

It identifies where vector control is needed. Under Annex 5, WHO publishes on a regular basis a list of areas where disinsection or other vector control measures are recommended for conveyances arriving from them, through temporary or standing recommendations.

It advises methods and materials. Where WHO has advised methods for disinsection, deratting, disinfection or decontamination, those should be used unless the competent authority is satisfied that others are as safe and reliable (Article 27), and States should accept measures applied elsewhere by WHO-advised methods.

It certifies and publishes. On a State Party's request WHO may, after appropriate investigation, certify that a port meets the IHR requirements (Article 20(4)), publishes certification guidelines and the list of certified ports (20(5)), and publishes the lists of authorized ports notified by States Parties (20(3)).

It provides technical guidance - notably the WHO Handbook for inspection of ships and issuance of ship sanitation certificates - and declares Public Health Emergencies of International Concern with temporary recommendations.
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare - the health authority for IHR purposes, under which the National IHR Focal Point sits.

Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), and under it the Port Health Organisation, headed by the Port Health Officer - the competent authority at the point of entry. It inspects ships, baggage, cargo and containers, supervises control measures and issues the ship sanitation certificates, working under the Indian Port Health Rules, 1955 with the IHR 2005.
Directorate General of Shipping, through its Maritime Health Branch, on the seafarer side - approving medical examiners and governing seafarers' medical fitness examination and certification.
Port authorities and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways support these functions at the ports themselves.

Ship Sanitation Control Exemption Certificate (SSCEC) - issued where the competent authority is satisfied that the ship is free of infection and contamination, including vectors and reservoirs, so that no control measures are required (Article 39(6)).

Ship Sanitation Control Certificate (SSCC) - issued where control measures were required and have been satisfactorily completed, and it records the evidence found and the measures taken (Article 39(5)). Under Annex 5 the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them are recorded on this certificate. If a satisfactory result could not be obtained, the authority notes that on the certificate (Article 39(7)).

blocks.p: Both follow the model in Annex 3, and they replaced the former Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates. Alongside them the master submits a Ship Declaration of Health under Article 37, to the model in Annex 8 - a declaration, not a certificate. Separately, and concerning the crew rather than the ship, seafarers hold medical fitness certificates under MLC 2006 and STCW.

blocks.h: 5. Issue in India, validity and extension - the ship

ul: In India they are issued by the Port Health Officer at a port authorized for the purpose and notified to WHO. Under Article 20(3) a State Party notifies which ports may issue the SSCC, which may issue the SSCEC only, and which may grant the one-month extension.
Validity: a maximum of six months, for both the SSCEC and the SSCC (Article 39(1)).
Extension: by one month, where the inspection or the required control measures cannot be accomplished at that port - the extension carries the ship to a port where the certificate can be obtained.

Where no valid certificate is produced, or evidence of a public health risk is found on board, the State Party may proceed under Article 27(1) - treating the ship as affected and requiring disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Control measures are to be carried out whenever possible when the ship and holds are empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading (Article 39(4)).

For Indian coastal trade calling where no Port Health Officer is available, DG Shipping has provided for a Statement of Compliance issued by an authorized medical examiner, to be endorsed at the earliest available opportunity.

blocks.h: 6. The crew's medical certificate, validity and extension

blocks.p: The stem's first sentence names the ship and the crew, and asks for the certificates "in India" without confining them to the ship. The seafarer's own certificate therefore belongs in the answer, and it has its own validity and its own extension - which is what makes it worth the marks.

ul: The certificate. A medical fitness certificate under MLC 2006 Regulation 1.2 and Standard A1.2. Standard A1.2(3) provides that a certificate issued under STCW is accepted for these purposes, so a single examination satisfies both instruments.

Who issues it. A duly qualified medical practitioner, or, for a certificate concerning eyesight alone, a person recognized by the competent authority as qualified to issue it (A1.2(4)). In India that means a medical examiner approved by the Directorate General of Shipping, which acts under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the rules made under it.

Validity. A maximum of two years; one year where the seafarer is under 18; and a certification of colour vision, a maximum of six years (A1.2(7)). These are maxima - a shorter period may be required by the specific duties or under STCW, and a State may set shorter periods.

Extension. Where a certificate expires in the course of a voyage it continues in force until the next port of call at which the seafarer can obtain a certificate from a qualified medical practitioner, provided the extension does not exceed three months (A1.2(9)). Separately, in urgent cases, the competent authority may permit a seafarer whose certificate has recently expired to work for a limited period (A1.2(8)).

blocks.p: So the answer to "validity and extension options" is two pairs of numbers, not one. The ship: six months, extendable by one month, by the Port Health Officer under the IHR. The crew: two years, extendable by up to three months to the next port, under MLC Standard A1.2. Different instrument, different authority, same shape of rule - and both extensions exist for the same practical reason, that a ship at sea cannot always reach the person who issues the document.

Three questions are asked and each must be visibly answered - WHO's role, the national agencies, and the certificates in India with their validity and extension. Take them in the printed order and head each one. The last limb carries the numbers the examiner is certainly looking for, so never let it be squeezed by a long essay on WHO. Note what this stem does not say: it asks for the certificates "in India", without the qualifier "issued to a vessel for maintenance of the ship in good health" that other sittings of this question print - and its own first sentence names "the ship and the crew". Read plainly, the crew's medical certificate is inside the task. Answer the ship's certificates first and fully, then give the crew's its own short paragraph. That way you are complete on the wider reading and lose nothing on the narrower one.

blocks.h: The currency point that will separate answers

blocks.p: The IHR were amended in 2024 and those amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025 - just two months before this paper was sat. One visible consequence: Article 37 is now the "Ship Declaration of Health". In the original 2005 text it was the "Maritime Declaration of Health", and that older name is what almost every textbook, coaching note and older syllabus still uses. Both texts were compared directly for this answer: the original uses "Maritime Declaration of Health" throughout and never the new name; the consolidated amended text uses "Ship Declaration of Health" throughout and never the old one. Using the current name, and being able to say why it changed, is a cheap and genuine mark.

blocks.h: Ship health and crew health are two different systems

blocks.p: The question asks about "the ship and the crew", and the two run on separate tracks with separate authorities. Ship health is WHO and the IHR, administered in India by the Port Health Organisation under DGHS and the Ministry of Health, and evidenced by the SSCC or SSCEC. Crew health is MLC 2006 and STCW, administered in India by DG Shipping through approved medical examiners, and evidenced by seafarers' medical fitness certificates. Candidates routinely put DG Shipping in charge of ship sanitation certificates. It is not - the Port Health Officer issues those.

ul: Calling the SSCC/SSCEC a Deratting Certificate. Those were the predecessors under the earlier Regulations and were replaced under the IHR 2005 - the scope widened from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.
Saying the certificates are valid for six months extendable by six months. The extension is one month, and only where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at that port.
Confusing the SSCC with the SSCEC. Exemption means no measures were needed; Control means measures were required and were completed.
Treating the Ship Declaration of Health as a certificate. It is a declaration by the master, to the Annex 8 model, and a State may dispense with it entirely under Article 37(4).
Naming WHO as an enforcement body. WHO recommends, certifies ports on request and publishes; the competent authority at the point of entry enforces.

blocks.p:
"Your certificate expired yesterday and the port cannot inspect - what happens?" The one-month extension in Article 39(1) exists precisely for this, and under Article 20(3)(c) States notify which of their ports may grant it, so that the ship can reach a port where the certificate is obtainable.

"When should the inspection be done?" Whenever possible with the ship and holds empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading - Article 39(4). Answering "any time" misses a printed requirement.

"What does WHO actually do about mosquitoes?" It publishes the list of areas where vector control is recommended for conveyances arriving from them, and advises the methods. States Parties then run vector control programmes at points of entry - to a minimum distance of 400 metres from the operational areas under Annex 5.

ul: Who issues the SSCC in India? The Port Health Officer, at a port authorized for the purpose and notified by India to WHO.
Under which ministry does the Port Health Organisation sit? The Directorate General of Health Services, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Validity and extension? Maximum six months; extendable by one month where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at the port.
What is recorded on an SSCC? The evidence found and the control measures taken - including, under Annex 5, the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them.
What happens if you cannot produce a valid certificate? The State Party may treat the ship as affected under Article 27(1) and require disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Which convention covers the crew's medical fitness rather than the ship's sanitation? MLC 2006, with STCW for certification - administered in India by DG Shipping.

blocks.p: RULE - AGENCY - PAPER - TWO CLOCKS. Rule: IHR 2005 as amended, WHO's role (steps 1 to 2). Agency: MoHFW, DGHS, Port Health Organisation and the Port Health Officer, with DG Shipping on the crew side (step 3). Paper: SSCEC, SSCC and the Ship Declaration of Health (step 4). Two clocks, and this is the part that answers the printed words 'validity and extension options': the ship runs on six months plus one (step 5); the crew runs on two years plus three months (step 6). Same idea, different numbers, different authority.

ul: International Health Regulations (2005), as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024; the 2024 amendments in force 19 September 2025

IHR Article 20(3) - States notify WHO of ports authorized to issue the SSCC, to issue the SSCEC only, and to grant the one-month extension; Article 20(4)-(5) - WHO certification of ports and certification guidelines

IHR Article 27(1) - affected conveyances: disinfect, decontaminate, disinsect or derat
IHR Article 37 - Ship Declaration of Health, model in Annex 8 (titled Maritime Declaration of Health in the original 2005 text)

IHR Article 39 - ship sanitation certificates: 39(1) six months, extendable by one month; 39(3) model in Annex 3; 39(4) ship and holds empty, in ballast before loading; 39(5) SSCC on completion of measures; 39(6) SSCEC where free of infection and contamination; 39(7) note where a satisfactory result cannot be obtained
IHR Annex 3 - model ship sanitation certificates; Annex 8 - model Ship Declaration of Health
IHR Annex 5 - vector-borne diseases: WHO list of areas, recording of vectors on the SSCC, and vector control programmes to a minimum of 400 metres from point of entry operational areas
Indian Port Health Rules, 1955, read with the IHR 2005; DG Shipping Order 10 of 2018 (revised) for the Statement of Compliance route

blocks.p: The IHR content in this answer is primary-verified, read in the consolidated WHO text as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024, and the renaming of the Declaration of Health was confirmed by reading the original 2005 text alongside it rather than by inference. Two areas are weaker. The Indian administrative detail - the position of the Port Health Organisation under DGHS, the Indian Port Health Rules 1955, and the DG Shipping Statement of Compliance route for coastal trade - rests on Government and classification-society restatements rather than on the order and rules texts themselves, and is stated at that level of confidence. The list of authorized Indian ports is deliberately not reproduced: it is notified by the State Party to WHO and changes, so naming ports in a study answer would date badly. A candidate asked for specifics should say that the list is notified to and published by WHO rather than guess at it.

blocks.h: Two clocks, and why the examiner set the word "options"

blocks.p: The printed words are "validity and extension options" - plural. On this stem that plural has a real answer, because two different certificate regimes are in play and each has its own pair of numbers. The ship runs on the IHR: six months, extended by one month, and the extension exists so that a ship can reach a port where the inspection can actually be done. The crew runs on MLC Standard A1.2: two years (one if under 18, six for colour vision), extended by up to three months to the next port of call where a practitioner is available. Notice that the two extensions are built on the same idea - the document expires while the ship is somewhere the issuer is not - and that neither is a favour: both are capped, and both run to the next place the thing can be done properly. If you can set those two side by side in three lines you have answered the last limb completely, and very few candidates will.

blocks.h: Do not put DG Shipping in charge of the ship

blocks.p: This is the error that costs most marks on the India limb, and the widened certificate limb on this paper makes it easier to fall into, because both authorities now appear in the same answer. Keep them apart: the Port Health Officer, under the Port Health Organisation, DGHS and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, certifies the ship - SSCC and SSCEC, under the IHR and the Indian Port Health Rules 1955. DG Shipping, under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, approves the medical examiners who certify the seafarer. Health ministry for the hull; shipping administration for the man. Write that sentence and the limb is safe.

questions.understand_first: There are two health systems on a ship and the question runs across both. One protects the world from the ship - vectors, infection and contamination crossing borders in a hull - and that is WHO's International Health Regulations, enforced by a port health authority and evidenced by a ship sanitation certificate. The other protects the crew, and that is labour and training law administered by the shipping administration. Keeping those two apart is what makes the India limb straightforward: the Port Health Officer certifies the ship, DG Shipping certifies the seafarer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long are ship sanitation certificates valid, and what extension is available?
retrieval_cards.answer: A maximum of six months, for both the SSCC and the SSCEC. Extendable by one month where the inspection or the required control measures cannot be accomplished at the port. IHR Article 39(1).
retrieval_cards.why: The single most examined fact in this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the SSCC from the SSCEC.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Exemption Certificate is issued where the authority is satisfied the ship is free of infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs, so no measures are needed. The Control Certificate is issued where measures were required and satisfactorily completed, and records the evidence found and the measures taken.
retrieval_cards.why: Exemption means nothing was needed; Control means something was done.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is Article 37 called now, and what was it called before?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Ship Declaration of Health, to the model in Annex 8. In the original 2005 text it was the Maritime Declaration of Health. The change came with the amendments in force from 19 September 2025.
retrieval_cards.why: Most textbooks and coaching notes still use the old name.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are these still called Deratting Certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates of the earlier Regulations were replaced under the IHR 2005 by the SSCC and SSCEC, widening the scope from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who issues ship sanitation certificates in India?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Port Health Officer, at a port authorized for the purpose and notified by India to WHO. The Port Health Organisation sits under the Directorate General of Health Services, within the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and works under the Indian Port Health Rules 1955 with the IHR 2005.
retrieval_cards.why: Not DG Shipping - that side handles seafarer medical fitness.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Summarise WHO's role in four verbs.
retrieval_cards.answer: It prescribes (the Regulations and the Annex 3 and 8 models), publishes (areas where vector control is recommended, and lists of authorized ports), advises (methods and materials for disinsection and deratting) and certifies (ports, on the State Party's request, under Article 20(4)).
retrieval_cards.why: WHO does not enforce - the competent authority at the point of entry does.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What distance does Annex 5 set for vector control programmes at points of entry?

retrieval_cards.why: A precise, checkable figure that shows the Annex has been read.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When should the sanitation inspection be carried out?
retrieval_cards.answer: Whenever possible when the ship and holds are empty, and in the case of a ship in ballast, before loading. IHR Article 39(4).
retrieval_cards.why: A printed requirement candidates routinely miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: No valid certificate is produced on arrival - what may the State Party do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Proceed under Article 27(1): treat the conveyance as affected and disinfect, decontaminate, disinsect or derat it, or have that done under its supervision, with isolation or quarantine if necessary.
retrieval_cards.why: Article 39(2) makes the cross-reference explicit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long is a seafarer's medical certificate valid, and what extension is available?
retrieval_cards.answer: A maximum of two years under MLC 2006 Standard A1.2(7); one year if the seafarer is under 18; and a certification of colour vision a maximum of six years. These are maxima - a shorter period may be required by the duties concerned or under STCW. Where a certificate expires in the course of a voyage it continues in force until the next port of call at which the seafarer can obtain one from a qualified medical practitioner, provided the extension does not exceed three months (A1.2(9)). In urgent cases a recently expired certificate may be allowed for a limited period (A1.2(8)).
retrieval_cards.why: This stem asks for the certificates 'in India' without confining them to the ship, and names the crew in its first sentence - so this is the second pair of validity and extension figures the printed word 'options' is asking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian authority certifies the ship's health, and which certifies the seafarer's?

The seafarer: a medical examiner approved by the Directorate General of Shipping, which acts under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, issuing the medical fitness certificate under MLC 2006 Standard A1.2 and STCW.
retrieval_cards.why: Health ministry for the hull, shipping administration for the man. Candidates routinely put DG Shipping in charge of ship sanitation certificates.
