blocks.h: 1. The framework these processes sit inside

blocks.p: A ship using LNG as fuel is designed and operated under SOLAS chapter II-1 part G and the IGF Code; the bunkering operation itself is specified by ISO 20519 - equipment, procedures, competence and documentation. Safety rests on a two-stage emergency shutdown system, with the delivery facility and the receiving ship joined by an ESD link so both act together. Before transfer, a safety zone is set, compatibility and mooring agreed, and the checklist and bunkering plan completed.

Carried out when a tank is being brought back into service after refit, repair or inerting - before any liquid is introduced. The tank is full of inert gas or nitrogen, and that atmosphere must be replaced with methane vapour.

ul: Why. Any carbon dioxide in inert gas would freeze at LNG temperature and block valves, filters and lines. Nitrogen does not freeze but is non-condensable: it accumulates in the vapour space, raises tank pressure, degrades the fuel's calorific value and upsets reliquefaction and gas supply.

How. LNG is taken from the supply through a vaporiser to produce warm methane vapour, which is admitted at the top of the tank. Being lighter than nitrogen, it forms a layer that pushes the heavier inert gas down and out through the bottom liquid line.
Where it goes. The displaced gas is led to the vent mast with attention to dispersion, or returned to the supply.

Completion. Sampling at the outlet continues until the hydrocarbon content reaches the specified value and carbon dioxide falls below its limit. The figures are set by the ship's manual and the containment system, not by a universal rule.

blocks.p: Once the tank holds methane vapour it is still warm. Cooling down brings the tank, pipework and manifold gradually towards LNG temperature, about minus 162 degrees Celsius, before bulk filling begins.

ul: Why. To avoid thermal shock and excessive thermal stress in the tank structure and insulation; and to avoid the violent flash-off that occurs when LNG meets warm surfaces, which would over-pressurise the tank and swamp the vapour handling capacity.
How. LNG is admitted in small controlled quantities through spray nozzles at the top of the tank, evaporating as it falls and cooling the structure evenly.

Rate control. The permitted rate of temperature fall is limited by the tank designer and class, and temperatures are watched at fixed sensors through the tank to keep the structure cooling uniformly rather than locally.
Completion. When the sensors reach the target and are stable, bulk transfer starts at a low initial rate and is ramped up only once pressures and temperatures are seen to be steady.

blocks.p: LNG boils continuously from heat ingress, and filling a tank displaces the vapour already in it. Vapour management is the control of tank pressure within the design limit throughout, and it is the process that actually governs how fast bunkering can proceed.

ul: Vapour return line - the primary method. A connection back to the bunker source returns the displaced vapour to its tanks, balancing pressure on both sides and removing the need to vent to atmosphere.
Consumption - burning the gas in the ship's engines, boilers or generators where the plant is running.
Reliquefaction where fitted, returning boil-off to the tank as liquid.
Gas combustion unit - burning off surplus gas safely where it cannot be used.
Controlled venting to the vent mast - a last resort only, because released methane is a potent greenhouse gas and venting is operationally and environmentally constrained.

Supporting controls. Spray filling to condense vapour; monitoring against the relief valve setting; level alarms and ESD trips; and attention to stratification and rollover where LNG of a different density is loaded onto an existing heel.

blocks.p: The emergency release system exists so that the transfer connection can be parted quickly and without spilling if the two vessels move beyond safe limits, if moorings fail, or in fire. Its heart is the emergency release coupling - a dry-break coupling with interlocked isolating valves which close before the halves separate, so the liquid held in the line is contained and the release of LNG and gas is minimised.

ul: ESD-1 - stop the pumps and close the manifold valves on both sides. Transfer ceases. Triggered manually from either end or automatically by tank level, pressure, gas detection or fire.
Drain and reduce inventory in the transfer line so far as the time available allows.

ESD-2 - the release stage. The coupling's isolating valves close first, then the coupling parts at its designed point. Initiation is manual, or automatic from mooring load or vessel position monitoring exceeding its limits.
After release - both sides are purged with nitrogen, the parted hose end is made safe, and personnel stay clear of the release zone while residual liquid boils off.

Before transfer the ESD link must be connected and function-tested, the coupling confirmed armed and certified, communications and agreed emergency signals established, and the release covered in the bunkering plan and drilled.

blocks.p: Four processes are named, so the examiner is marking four visible blocks. The commonest way to lose marks here is to write one long essay on LNG bunkering and leave the marker hunting for the four headings. Head each one exactly as printed. One short framing paragraph first is worth having - it lets you name the IGF Code, ISO 20519 and the ESD link once, so all four processes can then refer back to them without repetition.

blocks.h: The idea that ties the four together

blocks.p: Three of the four are about vapour and temperature, not liquid. That is the whole point. In LNG work the danger is rarely the liquid sitting in a tank - it is the gas you create by doing something too fast. Gassing up removes an atmosphere that would freeze or accumulate; cooling down prevents the flash-off that a warm tank would produce; vapour management disposes of the gas that filling inevitably generates. The emergency release is the fourth because it accepts that despite all of that, the connection may still have to be broken - and even then the design goal is the same, to part the line without releasing what is inside it. The order is also the order of the operation: you cannot cool a tank you have not gassed up, and you cannot fill one you have not cooled.

blocks.h: Why gassing up comes before cooling down

blocks.p: Because the freezing problem has to be solved while everything is still warm. Inert gas from a generator carries carbon dioxide, which becomes a solid well above LNG temperature. Introduce liquid into a tank that still holds carbon dioxide and you produce dry ice inside valves, strainers and spray lines - exactly where you least want a blockage. Gassing up removes it first. Nitrogen is a gentler problem but a persistent one: it will not freeze, but because it does not condense it stays in the vapour space, builds pressure, and thins the gas going to the engines. So gassing up is not a formality before the real work; it is what makes the cooling stage survivable.

ul: Reversing the order - cooling down before gassing up. Liquid must not enter a tank still holding inert gas.
Saying gassing up removes air. Air was removed earlier by inerting; gassing up removes the inert gas or nitrogen and replaces it with methane vapour.
Describing cooling down as "filling slowly". It is spray cooling through nozzles at a controlled rate of temperature fall, not a slow bulk fill.
Treating venting as normal vapour management. It is a last resort; the vapour return line is the primary route and methane venting carries a real environmental penalty.
Describing the emergency release coupling as a hose that simply breaks. Its defining feature is the interlocked isolating valves that close before separation.
Conflating ESD-1 and ESD-2. Stopping the transfer and parting the connection are two different stages, and ESD-2 follows ESD-1.

blocks.p:
"Why not use inert gas from the generator and go straight to loading?" Carbon dioxide in the inert gas freezes at LNG temperature and blocks the system. That single sentence is what the gassing-up limb is really testing.

"What limits how fast you can bunker?" Not the pump - the vapour handling capacity and the tank pressure limit. Bunkering is paced by where the gas can go.

"The bunker vessel starts to drift. What happens first?" ESD-1 stops the transfer and closes the manifold valves; only then does ESD-2 operate the release coupling. Going straight to "the hose disconnects" misses the sequence.

"You loaded a different LNG on top of your heel. What is the risk?" Stratification and rollover - a sudden mixing of layers of different density releasing a large volume of vapour and spiking tank pressure.

ul: What is the purpose of gassing up? To displace inert gas or nitrogen with methane vapour before liquid is admitted, chiefly to remove carbon dioxide that would freeze.
Why is warm vapour admitted at the top of the tank? It is lighter than nitrogen, so it layers above and pushes the heavier gas out through the bottom line.
What is the approximate temperature of LNG? About minus 162 degrees Celsius at atmospheric pressure.
What is the primary route for displaced vapour during bunkering? The vapour return line back to the bunkering facility.
What does an emergency release coupling do that an ordinary quick-release does not? Its interlocked isolating valves close before the coupling parts, containing the line inventory.
What links the two ESD systems? A ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore ESD link, so that shutdown on either side acts on both.

blocks.p: CLEAN - CHILL - CONTROL - CUT. Clean the atmosphere (step 2, gassing up). Chill the structure (step 3, cooling down). Control the pressure (step 4, vapour management). Cut the connection safely if it all goes wrong (step 5, emergency release). Step 1 is the framework they all sit in. The four Cs run in the same order as the operation itself.

ul: SOLAS chapter II-1 part G and the IGF Code (resolution MSC.391(95)) - design, arrangement and operation of ships using gases or other low-flashpoint fuels
ISO 20519 - Specification for bunkering of liquefied natural gas fuelled vessels: equipment, procedures, competence, documentation and the LNG bunker delivery note
ISO 20519 - the emergency release system shall consist of an emergency release coupling including interlocked isolating valves to minimize loss of LNG or natural gas on activation
ISO 20519 - the delivery facility and receiving vessel ESD systems shall be interconnected by a ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore ESD link for coordinated operation
ISO 20519 - the vapour return line as the connection returning excess vapour to the bunkering facility, removing the need to vent to atmosphere
Industry society guidance on gas as a marine fuel, and classification-society best-practice guidance on LNG bunkering, for the operational sequence, safety zone and checklists
Ship-specific documents: the containment system manual, the bunkering plan and the ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore checklist, which set the actual completion criteria and rates

blocks.p: The emergency release architecture and the vapour return function are primary-verified against ISO 20519 - the interlocked isolating valves within the coupling, and the interconnected ESD link, are that standard's own requirements. Two areas are weaker and are stated at their real strength. MIW holds no licensed copy of the IGF Code, so the framework statements rest on IMO and classification-society material rather than on the code text. And the numbers deliberately are not fixed: the hydrocarbon and carbon dioxide percentages that end gassing up, and the permitted rate of temperature fall during cooldown, are set by the containment system designer, the class rules and the ship's own manual, and vary between membrane and independent tank types. They are described as parameters to be read off the ship's documents rather than reduced to a single figure that would be wrong on most ships. ISO 20519 also exists in more than one edition; the requirements used here are those consistent across editions, and no clause numbers are cited. Finally, the ESD-1 then ESD-2 ordering is presented as the standard arrangement, because the precise trigger logic is set by the equipment maker's design and by the agreed bunkering plan.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: If you are revising this paper as a whole, read this question against Q2, the propeller-curve question. They look unrelated and they are not. Everything in limbs (a) to (c) exists to control the rate at which gas is generated and disposed of, because the bunkering operation is paced by vapour, not by liquid. The same logic governs a gas-fuelled main engine in service: a fouled hull or a heavy sea drives the engine into the torque-rich region, where it demands more fuel at a lower speed - and on a gas engine that demand runs straight into the fuel-gas supply system's pressure and temperature limits, with knock and misfire as the symptoms rather than exhaust temperature and smoke. In both cases the fuel system, not the fuel tank, is the constraint. Being able to say that in one sentence is the difference between two memorised procedures and an understanding of gas-fuelled operation.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Framework: SOLAS II-1 part G and the IGF Code for the ship; ISO 20519 for the bunkering operation; a two-stage ESD with the delivery facility and receiving ship joined by an ESD link. GASSING UP - before any liquid: replace inert gas or nitrogen with methane vapour, because carbon dioxide in inert gas FREEZES at LNG temperature and blocks the system, and nitrogen is non-condensable and builds pressure. LNG through a vaporiser, warm vapour admitted at the TOP, heavier inert gas pushed out at the bottom to the vent mast; stop when hydrocarbon content is up and carbon dioxide is down to the ship's specified values. COOLING DOWN - spray LNG through top nozzles at a controlled rate of temperature fall to about minus 162 degrees, to avoid thermal shock and the flash-off a warm tank would produce; then bulk fill at a low initial rate. VAPOUR MANAGEMENT - vapour return line first; then consumption, reliquefaction or a gas combustion unit; venting is a LAST RESORT. Watch tank pressure against the relief setting, level trips, and rollover when loading onto a heel of different density. EMERGENCY RELEASE - ESD-1 stops pumps and closes manifold valves; ESD-2 then closes the coupling's INTERLOCKED ISOLATING VALVES BEFORE the halves part, so the line inventory is contained; purge with nitrogen and secure the parted end. The ESD link must be function-tested before transfer.
critical_numbers: LNG is carried at about minus 162 degrees Celsius at atmospheric pressure
Cooldown rate is limited to the maximum rate of temperature fall set by the tank designer and class - a ship-specific figure, not a universal one
Gassing-up completion is judged on hydrocarbon and carbon dioxide percentages specified in the ship's manual for that containment system
Two ESD stages: ESD-1 stops transfer, ESD-2 releases the coupling
quick_revision.critical_regulation: ISO 20519 - the emergency release system shall consist of an emergency release coupling including interlocked isolating valves to minimize loss of LNG or natural gas on activation, with the delivery facility and receiving vessel ESD systems interconnected by a ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore ESD link
quick_revision.major_trap: Reversing the order, or thinking gassing up removes air. Air went out at inerting; gassing up removes the inert gas or nitrogen, chiefly because carbon dioxide would freeze at LNG temperature. Second trap: treating venting as normal vapour management - the vapour return line is the primary route and venting is a last resort.

questions.understand_first: Three of these four processes are about vapour and temperature, not liquid, and that is the key to the whole question. In LNG work the hazard is rarely the liquid sitting in a tank - it is the gas you generate by doing something too quickly. Gassing up removes an atmosphere that would freeze solid or refuse to condense; cooling down prevents the violent boil-off a warm tank would produce; vapour management disposes of the gas that filling inevitably creates, and is what actually paces the transfer. The fourth accepts that the connection may still have to be broken, and even then the design aim is unchanged: part the line without releasing what is inside it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the LNG bunkering question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the framework - IGF Code, ISO 20519, the ESD link. 2 gassing up. 3 cooling down. 4 vapour management. 5 the emergency release coupling procedure.
retrieval_cards.why: Framing first, then the four printed processes in the printed order.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must a tank be gassed up before LNG is admitted?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because carbon dioxide in inert gas freezes solid at LNG temperature and would block valves, strainers and spray lines; and nitrogen, while it will not freeze, is non-condensable, so it accumulates in the vapour space, raises pressure and thins the gas supplied to the engines.
retrieval_cards.why: The freezing point is what the limb is really testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is gassing up carried out, and why at the top of the tank?
retrieval_cards.answer: LNG is passed through a vaporiser to give warm methane vapour, admitted at the top of the tank. Methane vapour is lighter than nitrogen, so it layers above and pushes the heavier inert gas down and out through the bottom liquid line to the vent mast or back to the supply.
retrieval_cards.why: Density difference is what makes the displacement work.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is cooling down for, and how is it done?
retrieval_cards.answer: To bring tank, pipework and manifold gradually to about minus 162 degrees Celsius, avoiding thermal shock to the structure and the violent flash-off that LNG produces on warm surfaces. Done by spraying small controlled quantities of LNG through nozzles at the top, within the rate of temperature fall set by the designer and class.
retrieval_cards.why: Spray cooling at a controlled rate, not a slow bulk fill.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Rank the routes for vapour during bunkering.
retrieval_cards.answer: Vapour return line to the bunker source first; then consumption in engines, boilers or generators; then reliquefaction where fitted; then a gas combustion unit for surplus. Controlled venting to the vent mast is a last resort only, because methane is a potent greenhouse gas.
retrieval_cards.why: Venting last is the point - it is not routine practice.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes an emergency release coupling different from an ordinary quick-release?
retrieval_cards.answer: Its interlocked isolating valves close before the two halves separate, so the liquid held in the transfer line is contained and the loss of LNG or natural gas on activation is minimised.
retrieval_cards.why: The valves, not the parting, are the safety feature.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the emergency release sequence.
retrieval_cards.answer: ESD-1 stops the pumps and closes the manifold valves on both sides, ending transfer. Line inventory is drained as far as time allows. ESD-2 then closes the coupling's isolating valves and the coupling parts. Both sides purge with nitrogen and the parted end is secured.
retrieval_cards.why: Two stages, in order - stop first, part second.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What actually limits the rate at which a ship can be bunkered with LNG?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not the pump, but the vapour handling capacity and the tank pressure limit. The rate is paced by where the displaced and boil-off gas can go - principally the vapour return line - and by keeping pressure below the relief valve setting.
retrieval_cards.why: Bunkering speed is a vapour problem, not a liquid one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instruments govern LNG-fuelled ships and their bunkering?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS chapter II-1 part G with the IGF Code (resolution MSC.391(95)) for the ship's design, arrangement and operation; ISO 20519 for the bunkering operation, covering equipment, procedures, competence and the LNG bunker delivery note.
retrieval_cards.why: One for the ship, one for the transfer.

blocks.h: 1. What the Enhanced Survey Programme is

blocks.p: The ESP is a mandatory regime of intensified hull inspection for the two ship types whose structural failures have historically been catastrophic. It sits in the 2011 ESP Code, adopted as resolution A.1049(27) on 30 November 2011 and made compulsory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/2. Annex A covers bulk carriers, Annex B oil tankers, each split between single- and double-skin or double- and non-double-hull construction, and the Code is closely aligned with IACS Unified Requirement Z10.

It works by requiring, in addition to the ordinary periodical survey, a planned programme of close-up survey of critical structure within arm's reach, thickness measurement by an approved firm, and tank testing - all governed by a Survey Programme agreed with the Administration or its recognized organization before the renewal survey begins.

blocks.h: 2. What a Condition Assessment Programme survey is

blocks.p: CAP is a voluntary, additional classification-society service, carried out at the owner's request. Nothing in SOLAS or MARPOL requires it. Its purpose is commercial: it produces a numerical rating of the ship's actual condition, judged not against the minimum acceptable standard but against a new-build standard, and its scope is selectable - hull, machinery, cargo systems, or a combination. Owners buy it because charterers, oil-major vetting inspectors, buyers and financiers want an independent grading of an older ship, and it involves far more extensive gauging and testing than an ESP survey does.

blocks.p: In one line: ESP is a floor and CAP is a grade. CAP does not replace, extend or satisfy any statutory or class survey, and a good rating does not maintain class.

blocks.h: 4. Documents required to plan the survey

ul: The Survey Programme itself, developed by the owner and agreed with the Administration or RO before the survey begins, with the completed survey planning questionnaire.

Main structural plans of cargo and ballast tanks - scantling drawings, including identification of high-tensile steel, without which gauging results cannot be judged against the right diminution allowance.
Details of the means of access and the safe access plan (see below).
Evidence that the thickness measurement firm is approved by the society and its operators qualified.
The agenda and record of the survey planning meeting held before work starts between the attending surveyor, the owner's representative and the thickness measurement firm.
The Survey Report File - kept on board and at the owner's office - containing reports of structural surveys, the condition evaluation report and thickness measurement reports.
Previous repair history, and the history of cargoes and ballast carried, noting corrosive cargoes and tanks used for ballast.
Information on the corrosion prevention system - coating type and condition, anodes, and the standard of maintenance - together with the Coating Technical File for ballast tanks.
For tankers, the extent of inert gas plant use and the tank cleaning procedures followed.
Inspection reports by the ship's personnel on structural deterioration, fractures, leakage in bulkheads and piping, and coating breakdown.
Reports of port State control inspections recording structural deficiencies, and relevant safety management system records and non-conformities.
Any other information helping identify suspect areas and critical structural areas.

The means of access provided for each space and each area of close-up survey - permanent staging and walkways, temporary staging, rafts or boats, portable ladders, hydraulic arm vehicles, movable platforms, or remote inspection techniques where the society accepts them.
Confirmation that each means brings the surveyor within arm's reach of the structure to be examined.

The conditions attached to rafting - adequate clearance beneath the deckhead, controlled water level, lighting, attendance, lifejackets, and the requirement that the coating be in good condition with no structural failure in the space.
Enclosed space entry arrangements - ventilation, atmosphere testing for oxygen, hydrocarbons and toxic gases, gas-freeing, permit to work, standby personnel, and rescue equipment.
Lighting of an approved and adequate standard, and communication arrangements between the survey party and the responsible officer.
Cleaning and preparation - tanks cleaned, de-scaled and sufficiently free of water, sludge and residue for the structure to be seen.
Safety equipment and personal protective equipment, and the identity of the responsible person attending to supervise.
It is the owner who must provide the facilities for safe execution, and the surveyor may decline to proceed if they are not in place.

blocks.p: Three printed limbs, and the marks are unevenly available. Limb (a) is where the real discrimination happens, because the difference is conceptual, not a matter of listing two definitions. Limbs (b) and (c) are pure recall and reward organised lists - so give them structure rather than a stream of items. Splitting (b) into documents needed to plan and records of the ship's history and condition makes it far easier to write completely under pressure, and it is how the survey programme itself is organised.

ESP asks a pass/fail question; CAP asks a scoring question. The ESP exists to establish that the structure is still at or above the minimum standard the ship must meet to hold its certificates - a floor. CAP exists to say how far above that floor the ship actually sits, measured against a new-build standard - a grade. That single distinction generates every other difference: because ESP answers a legal question it is mandatory, flag-driven and hull-focused, and failure stops the ship trading. Because CAP answers a commercial question it is voluntary, owner-requested, scope-selectable, and failure costs charters rather than certificates.

blocks.h: The abbreviation trap that decides this question

blocks.p: CAP is not CAS. The Condition Assessment Programme is the voluntary classification-society grading described above. The Condition Assessment Scheme is a mandatory regime under MARPOL Annex I applying to single-hull oil tankers, adopted by IMO resolution. A candidate who answers limb (a) by describing CAS has answered the wrong question and has, worse, said that the thing is mandatory when the question is precisely about a voluntary scheme. If you are asked to distinguish ESP from CAP and you find yourself writing "MARPOL", stop - you have taken the wrong turning.

blocks.h: Why the paperwork in limb (b) exists

blocks.p: None of it is bureaucracy for its own sake, and saying why earns more than the list alone. A thickness reading is meaningless without the scantling drawing that says what the plate started at and whether it is high-tensile steel, because HTS carries a different diminution allowance. The cargo and ballast history tells the surveyor where to look, since a tank that has carried corrosive cargo or has been used for ballast corrodes differently. The coating condition and the Coating Technical File predict where wastage will appear next. And the Survey Report File makes the ship's structural condition a trend rather than a snapshot - which is the whole point of an enhanced programme.

ul: Describing CAP as a statutory requirement, or confusing it with the Condition Assessment Scheme under MARPOL Annex I.
Saying CAP replaces or extends class or statutory surveys. It does neither, and a good rating does not maintain class.
Saying the ESP applies to all ships. It applies to bulk carriers and oil tankers.
Omitting that the Survey Programme must be agreed before the survey starts, and that a planning meeting is held.

blocks.p:
"The owner has a CAP 1 rating. Can the special survey be relaxed?" No. CAP has no statutory effect whatever; the ESP survey stands in full.

"Which is more demanding?" In gauging volume and testing, CAP usually is - but it is the voluntary one. Demanding and mandatory are different axes, and that is the point of the comparison.

"When may a tank be rafted for close-up survey?" Only under conditions - clearance beneath the deckhead, controlled water level, adequate lighting and attendance, and the coating in good condition with no structural failure. "Whenever the tank is flooded" is wrong.

"Why does the surveyor want to know about high-tensile steel?" Because the permissible diminution differs, so the same measured thickness can be acceptable in one plate and a rejection in another.

ul: Which resolution is the ESP Code, and what makes it mandatory? Resolution A.1049(27), the 2011 ESP Code, made mandatory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/2.
Which ships does it apply to? Bulk carriers and oil tankers - Annex A and Annex B of the Code respectively.
What is a close-up survey? Examination of structural detail within arm's reach of the surveyor.
Who may carry out thickness measurement? A firm approved by the classification society, with qualified operators.
What is in the Survey Report File? Reports of structural surveys, the condition evaluation report and the thickness measurement reports.
Is CAP required by any convention? No. It is a voluntary classification-society service requested by the owner.
Who is responsible for safe access during survey? The owner, who must provide the facilities; the surveyor may decline to proceed without them.

What is weaker, and is stated at that level, is the detail. MIW holds no licensed copy of the ESP Code or of SOLAS, so the documentation list in limb (b) and the safe access content in limb (c) are assembled from classification-society restatements of the Code's survey programme requirements rather than read in the Code's own annexes; they are consistent across societies but they are not quoted from the instrument. Two figures are deliberately withheld. Gross tonnage thresholds for application are stated differently by different secondary sources, so the answer names the ship types and asserts no tonnage. And CAP rating scales, validity periods and scope options vary between classification societies, so the answer describes the common structure and says the detail is society-specific rather than presenting one society's scheme as universal. The distinction drawn between the Condition Assessment Programme and the MARPOL Annex I Condition Assessment Scheme is recorded deliberately, because the two abbreviations are routinely conflated and the error inverts the mandatory/voluntary answer the question is asking for.

blocks.h: This paper answers the other half of the question

blocks.p: Revise this question with Q1 of this same paper, which asks why bulk carriers were being lost in the early 1990s and what SOLAS chapter XII did about it. The two are the same subject approached from opposite ends. Chapter XII is the construction and operational answer to bulk carrier structural failure - damage stability with a flooded hold, strength of the transverse watertight bulkhead and double bottom, restrictions on loading. The Enhanced Survey Programme is the inspection answer to the same casualty record, which is why Annex A of the ESP Code is the bulk carrier annex and why the regime concentrates on close-up survey of side shell frames and end brackets in the cargo holds. A candidate who has seen both can say, in one sentence, that the ships were lost through corrosion and fatigue of side structure that nobody was required to look at closely, and that IMO responded by both strengthening the ship and mandating that somebody look.

questions.understand_first: The two regimes answer different questions, and everything else follows from that. The Enhanced Survey Programme asks whether the structure is still at or above the minimum standard the ship must meet to keep its certificates - a floor, checked because the law requires it. A Condition Assessment Programme survey asks how far above that floor the ship actually sits, measured against a new-build standard - a grade, bought because a charterer or a buyer wants an independent opinion on an ageing ship. So the more demanding survey of the two is usually the voluntary one, which feels backwards until you see that demanding and mandatory are separate axes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In one line, what is the difference between ESP and CAP?
retrieval_cards.answer: ESP is a floor and CAP is a grade. ESP establishes that the structure still meets the minimum acceptable standard; CAP scores actual condition against a new-build standard. One protects certification, the other protects employment.
retrieval_cards.why: Every other difference follows from this one.

retrieval_cards.answer: No. CAP has no statutory effect at all. It does not replace, extend or satisfy any statutory or class survey, and a good rating does not maintain class.
retrieval_cards.why: Owners sometimes argue otherwise; the answer is still no.

retrieval_cards.answer: The owner develops a Survey Programme, with the survey planning questionnaire, and it is agreed with the Administration or its recognized organization. retrieval_cards.why: Agreement before the survey, not during it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is in the Survey Report File?
retrieval_cards.answer: Reports of structural surveys, the condition evaluation report, and the thickness measurement reports. It is kept on board and at the owner's office, so that structural condition can be read as a trend rather than a snapshot.
retrieval_cards.why: The trend is the point of an enhanced programme.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does close-up survey mean, and why does high-tensile steel matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Close-up survey is examination of structural detail within arm's reach of the surveyor. High-tensile steel must be identified on the scantling drawings because it carries a different permissible diminution, so the same measured thickness may be acceptable in one plate and a rejection in another.
retrieval_cards.why: A gauging without the drawing is a number without a meaning.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When may a tank be rafted for close-up survey?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only under stated conditions - adequate clearance beneath the deckhead, controlled water level, adequate lighting, attendance and lifejackets, and the coating in good condition with no structural failure in the space. Not simply whenever the tank can be flooded.

blocks.h: 1. Secure the evidence and establish the facts

ul: Do not dress, grind or blend the crack. Material removed before assessment destroys the evidence class, the underwriter and the root-cause investigation all need.
Record it. Photographs and video with a scale in frame, and a dimensioned sketch.

Locate it precisely - blade number from the stamping on the boss, pressure or suction face, radial position as a fraction of the blade radius, distance from the leading or trailing edge and from tip and root, and the crack's length and orientation.
Examine the whole propeller, not just the one blade - the remaining blades, the leading and trailing edges, the tips, the boss, the keyway and the fairing cone. A crack is rarely isolated.
Look for related damage - rudder, stern frame, rope guard, stern tube seal, hull marks - which would point to contact or grounding.

Assemble the service history - vibration or unusual noise, shaft power and revolution anomalies, any grounding, ice contact or rope entanglement, stern tube oil analysis and the planned maintenance record.

Clean the area only as far as the surveyor permits, then carry out liquid dye penetrant testing. Propellers are cast in non-ferromagnetic alloys - nickel-aluminium bronze or manganese bronze - so magnetic particle inspection cannot be used. Where depth must be established, eddy current or ultrasonic techniques are applied.
Have the testing done by a qualified operator from an approved firm and obtain a written report.
Establish what the defect actually is: a genuine fatigue crack, a casting defect, or cavitation erosion pitting that resembles cracking. The three have different consequences and different causes.

Inform the Master first, then report to the Company - the technical superintendent and, under the ISM Code, the Designated Person Ashore - and raise it in the safety management system as a hazardous occurrence or non-conformity so that it enters the analysis and corrective-action process.

The report must be factual and complete: description and precise location, dimensions, NDT method and result, photographs and sketch, propeller particulars (maker, material, drawing and serial number, diameter and pitch), relevant service history, and the effect on the dry-dock programme and undocking date.

State the options and a recommendation, with the implications of each for cost and time - but recognise the division of responsibility: the Chief Engineer establishes the facts and recommends; the Company decides and instructs.
Request instructions, and confirm who will liaise with class, the repairer and the underwriter.

blocks.h: 4. Involve classification and settle the repair

ul: Notify the classification society and request the attending surveyor to examine. The owner is under a duty to report any damage or defect which affects or may affect classification, and concealing it puts class - and with it the statutory certificates and the insurance - at risk.

The surveyor assesses the crack against the society's rules. Acceptance depends heavily on where on the blade it lies: the highly stressed region is the most restricted and repairs there are limited or prohibited, while damage near the tip is treated far more permissively. ISO 484 governs the tolerances against which repaired geometry is judged.

The possible outcomes are: accept as found; grind out and blend to a smooth radius within permitted limits; weld repair by an approved procedure; crop and re-form; or replace the blade or the propeller.

Where a repair is done it must be by a class-approved repairer to an approved welding procedure with the pre-heat and post-weld heat treatment the alloy requires, followed by re-testing, a check of pitch and geometry, and static balancing.
Obtain the surveyor's endorsement. If the repair is deferred, expect a condition of class with a time limit rather than a clean survey.

Consider separately whether the occurrence is reportable to the flag Administration. That turns on its cause and on whether seaworthiness was affected - damage arising from a grounding or contact is reportable; wastage found at a routine docking generally is not.

blocks.h: 5. Insurance and preservation of the claim

ul: Through the Company, notify the hull and machinery underwriters, and the P&I club if any third-party element arises, and arrange attendance of the underwriter's surveyor before repairs begin.

Whether a claim lies depends on the cause. Damage from an insured peril such as contact or grounding is recoverable; ordinary wear and tear and cavitation erosion are not, and a latent defect is recoverable only so far as the policy provides for it.
Do not commit to a repair method or cost without the underwriter's agreement where a claim is contemplated, and retain removed material and samples for metallurgical examination.

Establish the cause: cavitation erosion; fatigue initiating at cavitation pitting or a casting defect acting as a stress raiser; impact with a submerged object or ice; dezincification of manganese bronze; galvanic attack where anodes or the impressed current system are defective; or sustained overload from heavy running or excessive astern working.
Act on it - review hull and propeller roughness, fouling and polishing intervals, confirm cathodic protection is functioning, monitor shaft vibration, and review astern working and heavy running.

Close the loop: file the NDT and survey reports, repair procedure, welder qualifications and balancing record; update the machinery history, planned maintenance system and underwater inspection schedule; feed the lessons through the safety management system; and hand over fully.

blocks.p: The command is state the steps, so the answer must be a sequence, not an essay about propellers. Six headed steps in a defensible order will outscore a longer piece of prose every time. Notice what the question actually asks: it is a management question with a technical trigger. The examiner wants to see that a Chief Engineer knows who must be told, in what order, and what must not be touched in the meantime. Metallurgy earns marks only where it changes a decision.

blocks.h: The instinct you have to suppress

blocks.p: The engineer's reflex on finding a surface crack in a dock, with the undocking date approaching, is to dress it out and carry on. That reflex is the most expensive mistake available here. Grinding the crack away before anyone has seen it destroys three things at once: the class surveyor's ability to assess what was actually there, the underwriter's ability to accept a claim, and the root-cause investigation that would stop it happening on the sister ship. The propeller can be repaired later; none of that evidence can be recovered. So the first step is not a repair step at all - it is to stop, record, and report.

blocks.h: Why location on the blade decides almost everything

blocks.p: A propeller blade is not uniformly stressed. Bending stress from thrust and torque is greatest towards the root, and the blade is thinnest towards the tip and the edges, so a crack of the same length means very different things depending on where it is. Classification rules divide the blade into zones accordingly: in the highly stressed region, welding is restricted or not permitted at all and the realistic outcomes are limited grinding or blade replacement; near the tip the same defect may be blended out without difficulty. This is why the answer must record blade number, face, radius and distance from the edge before anything else - those four facts, not the crack's length, are what determine the outcome.

ul: Proposing magnetic particle inspection. Propellers are nickel-aluminium or manganese bronze and are not ferromagnetic, so MPI simply does not work. Use dye penetrant.
Grinding or welding before class attends and before the extent is established.
Reporting to the Company but not to class, or assuming the superintendent will do it.
Treating every crack as a claim. Cavitation erosion and ordinary wear are not insured perils.
Deciding the repair yourself. The Chief Engineer recommends; the Company instructs and class approves.
Omitting balancing and geometry check after repair - a repaired blade that is out of pitch or out of balance introduces vibration and a new fatigue problem.
Stopping at the repair and never establishing the cause, which guarantees a repeat.

blocks.p:
"Why not MPI?" Because the material is not ferromagnetic. If you cannot answer this you have shown you have never actually stood at a propeller in a dock.

"The dock is due to flood tomorrow. What do you do?" Report and get class to attend. Commercial pressure does not change the sequence, and undocking with an unreported defect affecting class is a far worse outcome than a delay.

"Is this a general average or a hull claim?" Neither is automatic - it depends entirely on cause. Establish that first.

"You blended out the crack and it looked fine. Any problem?" Yes - the blade geometry and pitch may now be outside tolerance, the blade is out of balance with the others, and you have removed the evidence. Blending is permitted only within limits and with class agreement.

"Must you report it to the flag State?" It depends on cause and on whether seaworthiness was affected - not automatically.

ul: Which NDT method for a bronze propeller, and why? Dye penetrant - the alloy is not ferromagnetic, so magnetic particle inspection is unusable.
What four facts locate the defect? Blade number, pressure or suction face, radial position, and distance from the leading or trailing edge.
Who approves a propeller weld repair? The classification society, and it must be carried out by an approved repairer to an approved procedure.
What is done after a blade repair? Re-testing, a pitch and geometry check against tolerance, and static balancing.
What happens if the repair is deferred? A condition of class with a time limit may be imposed.
Name three causes of blade cracking. Cavitation erosion leading to fatigue, impact with a submerged object, and a casting defect acting as a stress raiser.
Who do you tell first on board? The Master, then the Company and the Designated Person Ashore.

blocks.p: STOP - TEST - TELL - CLASS - CLAIM - CAUSE. Stop and preserve the evidence (step 1). Test to establish what it really is (2). Tell the Master and the Company (3). Class attends and settles the repair (4). Claim - notify underwriters before repairing (5). Cause - find it, fix it, record it (6). The order matters and is itself examinable: everything that could destroy evidence comes after the people who need that evidence have been told.

ul: ISM Code - reporting and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences; the role of the Designated Person Ashore; the safety management system's corrective action process

Classification society rules - the owner's duty to report damage or defects affecting or which may affect classification; surveyor attendance; approved repairer and approved welding procedure; conditions of class
ISO 484 (parts 1 and 2) - shipbuilding propeller manufacturing tolerances, against which repaired geometry is judged
Class rules on propeller blade zones - the highly stressed region is the most restricted for repair; zone boundaries and permitted welding are society-specific

blocks.p: This answer is procedural rather than regulatory, and its provenance reflects that. The class relationship - the owner's duty to report damage affecting classification, surveyor attendance and approval of the repair - is carried from the verified QP2607 Q3 treatment of classification and the RO Code. The materials point is settled engineering: propeller alloys are not ferromagnetic, so magnetic particle inspection is unusable and dye penetrant is the standard surface method. What is deliberately not quoted is repair acceptance detail. MIW holds no licensed copy of any society's rules or of ISO 484, and blade zone boundaries and the extent of welding permitted in each differ between societies, so the answer states the principle - the highly stressed region is the most restricted, the tip region the least - rather than reproducing one society's zones as though they were universal. Two outcomes are also left open on purpose, because the question supplies no cause. Whether the occurrence is a reportable casualty to the Administration turns on cause and on whether seaworthiness was affected. Whether a hull and machinery claim lies turns on cause and on the policy wording. Asserting either would be inventing facts the examiner did not give, and the better answer states the test and applies it conditionally.

blocks.h: The other dock question on this paper

blocks.p: Read this against Q5, the Enhanced Survey Programme question, because between them they cover the two things that happen to a ship in a dry dock and they share one idea. Q5 is the planned examination - a survey programme agreed before the dock, close-up survey within arm's reach, thickness measurement by a firm approved by the society, all of it scheduled. This question is the unplanned finding, the thing nobody put in the docking specification. What the two have in common is the answer to who may do what: in both, the examination that counts must be carried out by a competent person the society recognises, and in both the Chief Engineer's job is to establish and preserve the facts - not to make the assessment himself, and certainly not to remove the evidence. On Q5 that means not gauging the plate yourself; here it means not grinding out the crack before the surveyor has seen it. Same principle, opposite ends of the docking list.

Grinding the defect away before it has been seen destroys three separate things at once - the class surveyor's assessment, the insurer's ability to accept a claim, and the root-cause work that would stop it recurring on the sister ship. The propeller can be repaired later; none of that evidence can be recovered. So this is not really a repair question. retrieval_cards.answer: 1 secure the evidence and establish the facts. 2 establish the nature and extent by NDT. 3 report to the Company. 4 involve classification and settle the repair. 5 insurance and preservation of the claim. 6 root cause, prevention and close-out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can magnetic particle inspection not be used on a propeller?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because marine propellers are cast in non-ferromagnetic alloys - nickel-aluminium bronze or manganese bronze - and magnetic particle inspection requires a ferromagnetic material. Liquid dye penetrant is the standard surface method, with eddy current or ultrasonic where depth must be established.
retrieval_cards.why: A single fact that shows whether the candidate has really been at a propeller.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must the crack not be ground out before class attends?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it simultaneously destroys the surveyor's ability to assess what was there, the underwriter's ability to accept a claim, and the root-cause investigation. The propeller can be repaired later; the evidence cannot be recovered.
retrieval_cards.why: The commercial pressure to do exactly this is the point of the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which four facts locate the defect?
retrieval_cards.answer: Blade number from the boss stamping; whether it is on the pressure or the suction face; the radial position as a fraction of blade radius; and the distance from the leading or trailing edge. These, not the crack's length, determine the repair outcome.
retrieval_cards.why: Position on the blade governs what class will permit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the owner's duty to the classification society here?
retrieval_cards.answer: To report any damage or defect which affects or may affect classification, and to have the surveyor attend. A repair requires an approved repairer working to an approved procedure, followed by re-examination, a geometry and pitch check, and balancing.
retrieval_cards.why: Concealment puts class, the statutory certificates and the insurance at risk.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who decides what happens to the propeller?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not the Chief Engineer. The CE establishes the facts, reports and recommends; the Company decides and instructs; the classification society approves the repair and endorses it. Confusing those roles is a management failure, not a technical one.
retrieval_cards.why: The question is about handling the situation, not fixing the blade.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must be done after a blade repair is completed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Re-testing by NDT, a check of pitch and blade geometry against tolerance, and static balancing - then the surveyor's endorsement. A repaired blade out of pitch or out of balance introduces vibration and a fresh fatigue problem.
retrieval_cards.why: The repair is not finished when the welding stops.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the likely causes of propeller blade cracking.
retrieval_cards.answer: Cavitation erosion, and fatigue initiating at cavitation pitting or at a casting defect acting as a stress raiser; impact with a submerged object or ice; dezincification of manganese bronze; galvanic attack where anodes or the impressed current system are defective; and sustained overload from heavy running or excessive astern working.
retrieval_cards.why: Cause drives both the insurance position and the prevention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is this automatically an insurance claim and a reportable casualty?
retrieval_cards.answer: Neither is automatic. Recoverability depends on cause and on the policy - an insured peril such as contact or grounding may be recoverable, while ordinary wear and cavitation erosion are not. Reportability to the Administration depends on the cause and on whether seaworthiness was affected.
retrieval_cards.why: The question gives no cause, so both must be stated as conditional.

blocks.h: 1. What the Convention is, and what it exists to do

blocks.p: The Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic, 1965 - the FAL Convention - was adopted on 9 April 1965 and entered into force on 5 March 1967. It is IMO's trade facilitation instrument, and it is the odd one out among the conventions a Chief Engineer meets: SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW tell you what the ship, its equipment and its people must be. FAL tells public authorities what they may demand of a ship when she arrives, stays and departs.

Its objectives, in the Organization's own words, are to prevent unnecessary delays in maritime traffic, to aid co-operation between Governments, and to secure the highest practicable degree of uniformity in formalities and other procedures. The problem it was written to solve was simple and expensive: every port demanded different documents, in a different format, in a different number of copies, and a ship could lose more time to paperwork than to cargo.

ul: The obligations sit in an annex, expressed as Standards - measures necessary and practicable in order to facilitate international maritime traffic - and Recommended Practices, measures the application of which is desirable.

A Contracting Government that finds it impracticable to comply with a Standard, or that considers it necessary to adopt differing requirements, must notify the Secretary-General of the difference (article VIII). The obligation is therefore not absolute, but a departure must be declared rather than simply operated.
The annex prescribes a maximum, not a minimum: under Standard 2.1bis public authorities shall not require more information than is provided for in the standardised declarations.

Those declarations are the FAL Forms 1 to 7 - the General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Ship's Stores Declaration, Crew's Effects Declaration, Crew List, Passenger List and Dangerous Goods manifest - together with the Declaration of Health and documents required under the Universal Postal Convention.
The annex is amended by tacit acceptance: adopted under article VII(2)(a) and deemed accepted under article VII(2)(b) unless a stated proportion of Contracting Governments object by a stated date.
Time is the cargo owner's money and the ship's cost. Port time is the least productive time a ship has; every hour saved at the interface is earned twice, once in charter and once in fuel.
Uniformity is what makes a ship tradeable worldwide. A master and crew cannot learn a different clearance regime for every port, and the FAL Forms mean they do not have to.
A ceiling on demands protects the ship from the port. Standard 2.1bis is a genuine protection: it limits what an authority may lawfully require.
It is the foundation the digital layer was built on. Nothing else could have been standardised electronically if the content had not first been standardised on paper.

blocks.h: 4. The recent amendments - what is actually in force

blocks.p: Two annex amendments matter at this point, and both are already in force.

ul: Resolution FAL.14(46), adopted 13 May 2022, in force 1 January 2024. This is the important one. It made the single window mandatory: under Standard 1.3quin as amended, public authorities shall introduce arrangements enabling all information required under Standard 2.1 to be provided to a single window by electronic means, and shall consider the single window as the channel for communicating their decisions. The annex defines a single window as an environment that allows for the submission or provision of standardized and harmonized information and declarations to a single entry point, typically by electronic means. It also carries Standards 2.1bis and 2.1.2 on the information ceiling and on pre-arrival and pre-departure information.

Resolution FAL.15(47), adopted 17 March 2023, in force 1 January 2025 - ten months before this examination. It amends Recommended Practice 7.11 on national facilitation programmes, requiring them to be established and maintained taking into account the need to combat illicit activities. It was adopted under article VII(2)(a) and its operative paragraph 2 determines, under article VII(2)(b), that it enters into force on 1 January 2025 unless one third of Contracting Governments objected before 1 October 2024. No such objection was made.

blocks.p: The single window was not a standing start. Electronic exchange of information had already become mandatory from 9 April 2019, with a minimum twelve-month transition; the 2022 amendments took the further step of requiring a single entry point rather than merely an electronic one.

blocks.h: 5. What is NOT yet an annex requirement

blocks.p: This distinction is worth marks and is easy to get wrong. The FAL 49 session (10 to 14 March 2025) approved a number of facilitation items - a Recommended Practice 6.24 on vaccinations and medical care, revised Maritime Single Window Guidelines, and a new edition of the IMO Compendium. Approved is not adopted, and adopted is not in force. Those items were not annex requirements at this point.

Nor are all recent FAL resolutions annex amendments at all. FAL.18(49) on mooring personnel and FAL.17(48) on wildlife smuggling are guidelines resolutions - adopted, but they do not alter a Standard or a Recommended Practice. So the accurate statement of the position is: the amendments to answer on are FAL.14(46) and FAL.15(47), and there is no annex amendment adopted and awaiting entry into force.

ul: One submission instead of many. Where a single window is properly implemented the ship's agent submits a harmonised data set once, and customs, immigration, port health, port authority and security each draw from it. The master's staff stop retyping the same crew list into five formats.

Standardised data, not merely electronic data. The IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business, developed with the World Customs Organization, UN/CEFACT and ISO, provides the harmonised reference data model - so that 'port of call' means the same field to every system. Without it, a single window would simply be a shared inbox.
Clearance moves off the critical path. Pre-arrival submission under Standard 2.1.2 means formalities can be completed before the ship is alongside, so berth time is spent working cargo.

Data protection becomes an operational concern. Concentrating crew, cargo and voyage data at one entry point raises the value of that point to an attacker, which is where facilitation meets cyber risk management.

The obligation falls on the AUTHORITY, not the ship. The Convention requires public authorities to establish and maintain the single window; the ship's benefit is derivative, and where a State has not implemented one the ship gains nothing - which is exactly the unevenness the Convention exists to reduce.

The environmental gain runs through TIME. Reliable, standardised pre-arrival information is what makes just-in-time arrival possible: if a ship knows when the berth will actually be free, she can reduce speed on passage instead of steaming hard to anchor and wait. Fuel burn falls with speed sharply, so waiting at sea at reduced power is materially cheaper in fuel and emissions than arriving early and idling.

It supports the emissions regime rather than duplicating it. The Convention sets no emissions standard and claims none; it removes an administrative obstacle to operating efficiently, which is a different and more modest kind of contribution.
Paper itself. Eliminating multi-copy paper declarations at every port is a real if small resource saving, and removes courier and physical-attendance movements at the ship-shore interface.
Better port planning reduces congestion, and congestion is idling main and auxiliary machinery at anchor - emissions produced for no transport work at all.

blocks.p: State the limit honestly, because the question says 'analyze'. The benefits above are conditional on implementation. A single window that is a web form wrapping the same seven paper documents delivers the compliance and none of the benefit; just-in-time arrival requires the charterparty to permit it, since a laytime regime that starts the clock on arrival rewards the ship for steaming hard and waiting. The Convention removes the administrative obstacle. The commercial obstacle is untouched by it.

blocks.h: 8. The limits - and what the Convention does not do

ul: It does not regulate the ship - no construction, equipment, manning or emission requirement.
It does not override customs, immigration or quarantine law; it standardises the interface with them.
It does not make a Recommended Practice binding. Only Standards carry the article VIII difference obligation.
It does not, by itself, deliver a working single window in any particular State.

blocks.p: Three tasks are set in one running stem and the third is the one that separates answers. Explain the objectives and importance; discuss the recent amendments; analyze their impact, particularly in relation to digitalization and sustainability. The examiner has named the two lenses, so give each its own heading - an answer that discusses 'modernisation' generally has not done what was asked. Budget roughly a third to the Convention itself and two thirds to amendments and impact, and make sure the word analyze is earned by saying where the benefit does not arrive.

blocks.h: The distinction that carries the amendment limb

blocks.p: Approved is not adopted, and adopted is not in force - and on the FAL Convention there is a fourth trap on top of those three: not every FAL resolution is an annex amendment. A resolution adopting guidelines changes no Standard and no Recommended Practice. So when a question asks for 'the recent amendments', the disciplined answer names the resolutions that actually amended the annex and says what each did - here FAL.14(46) and FAL.15(47) - rather than listing everything the Facilitation Committee has been busy with. Being able to say 'and there is no annex amendment currently adopted and awaiting entry into force' is worth more than an extra paragraph, because it shows you know the difference between a committee's work programme and the law.

blocks.h: The single window is an obligation on the STATE

blocks.p: This is the point most often inverted. Standard 1.3quin requires public authorities to introduce the arrangements and to treat the single window as the channel for communicating decisions. Nothing in it obliges the ship to do anything new; the ship's benefit is entirely derivative of the State having done its part. That is why the practical experience of the single window is so uneven port to port, and why an honest analysis has to say so. If you write that 'the FAL Convention requires ships to submit electronically to a single window', you have got the duty-holder wrong.

blocks.h: Where the sustainability marks actually are

blocks.p: Candidates reach for 'less paper' and stop. Less paper is real but trivial. The environmental argument runs through time and speed. Fuel consumption rises steeply with speed, so the difference between steaming hard to an anchorage and then waiting, and slowing down on passage to arrive when the berth is free, is a large fuel and emissions difference for the same voyage and the same cargo. Reliable standardised pre-arrival data is what makes that choice possible - which is how a trade facilitation convention ends up on a decarbonisation answer. Then add the limit: it only works if the charterparty lets it, because under a conventional laytime regime the ship is rewarded for arriving and tendering notice, not for arriving late and efficiently.

ul: Treating FAL as a safety or pollution convention. It regulates formalities, not the ship.
Saying the single window obliges the ship. It obliges public authorities.
Listing FAL Committee outputs as 'amendments' when they are guidelines resolutions or merely approved items.
Giving the adoption year as the operative date. Adopted 1965, in force 5 March 1967; the single window amendments in force 1 January 2024.
Claiming a percentage fuel saving for just-in-time arrival. The figures vary enormously with trade and port; explain the mechanism instead.
Answering 'impact' with advantages only. The command verb is analyze, and an analysis states the conditions under which the benefit fails to appear.

blocks.p:
"Which recent FAL amendment is in force and what did it change?" FAL.14(46), in force 1 January 2024, making the single window mandatory through Standard 1.3quin; and FAL.15(47), in force 1 January 2025, amending Recommended Practice 7.11 on national facilitation programmes.

"A port asks for a document not in the FAL Forms. Must you provide it?" Standard 2.1bis says public authorities shall not require more information than the standardised declarations provide for. If the State has notified a difference under article VIII, it may lawfully require more - which is why the difference is notified rather than simply operated.

"Is a Recommended Practice binding?" No. Only Standards carry the article VIII notification obligation; a Recommended Practice is a measure whose application is desirable.

"How is the annex amended?" Tacit acceptance - adopted under article VII(2)(a), deemed accepted under VII(2)(b) unless a stated proportion objects by a stated date. FAL.15(47) states it in operative words with both dates.

ul: When was the FAL Convention adopted and when did it enter into force? Adopted 9 April 1965; in force 5 March 1967.

What is the difference between a Standard and a Recommended Practice? A Standard is necessary and practicable and a difference must be notified under article VIII; a Recommended Practice is desirable.

Name the FAL declarations. General Declaration, Cargo, Ship's Stores, Crew's Effects, Crew List, Passenger List and Dangerous Goods - plus the Declaration of Health and Universal Postal Convention documents.
What is a single window? An environment allowing standardized and harmonized information and declarations to be submitted to a single entry point, typically electronically.
Who must provide it? The public authorities of the Contracting Government, under Standard 1.3quin as amended by FAL.14(46).
What is the IMO Compendium for? It is the harmonised reference data model, developed with the WCO, UN/CEFACT and ISO, so that the same data element means the same thing in every system.
How does a facilitation convention reduce emissions? By making just-in-time arrival possible, so a ship slows on passage instead of steaming hard and waiting at anchor.

blocks.p: WHAT - HOW - WHY, then TWO RESOLUTIONS and TWO LENSES. What: 1965, in force 1967, formalities not ships (step 1). How: Standards and Recommended Practices, article VIII differences, Forms 1 to 7, the 2.1bis ceiling (step 2). Why: time, uniformity, protection from excessive demands (step 3). Two resolutions: FAL.14(46) - 2022, in force 1 Jan 2024, single window mandatory, Standard 1.3quin; FAL.15(47) - 2023, in force 1 Jan 2025, Recommended Practice 7.11 (steps 4 to 5). Two lenses: digitalization - one submission, Compendium data model, clearance off the critical path (step 6); sustainability - just-in-time arrival, speed and fuel (step 7). Then the limit: implementation and the charterparty (step 8).

questions.understand_first: The FAL Convention is the one IMO instrument that does not regulate the ship. SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW tell you what the ship, her equipment and her people must be; FAL tells the shore what it may demand of the ship when she arrives, stays and departs. Once that is clear, everything else follows - why its obligations fall on public authorities rather than on the master, why its central provision is a ceiling on what may be required rather than a floor, and why a trade facilitation convention turns up in a discussion about emissions. The chain is short and worth holding: standardise the information, and it can be exchanged electronically; exchange it electronically to a single point, and clearance stops depending on the ship being alongside; make arrival times reliable, and the ship can slow down on passage instead of racing to wait. Paperwork to fuel, in four steps.

retrieval_cards.answer: No, and for two different reasons. The FAL 49 facilitation items - Recommended Practice 6.24 on vaccinations and medical care, the revised Maritime Single Window Guidelines and the new Compendium edition - were APPROVED ONLY, not adopted and not in force. FAL.18(49) on mooring personnel and FAL.17(48) on wildlife smuggling were adopted, but they are GUIDELINES resolutions and amend no Standard or Recommended Practice. The annex amendments to answer on are FAL.14(46) and FAL.15(47).
retrieval_cards.why: Approved is not adopted, adopted is not in force, and not every resolution is an amendment. Three separate distinctions in one question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the FAL annex amended?
retrieval_cards.answer: By tacit acceptance. Amendments are adopted under article VII(2)(a) and the resolution then determines, under article VII(2)(b), that they enter into force on a stated date unless at least one third of Contracting Governments notify the Secretary-General in writing before an earlier stated date that they do not accept them. FAL.15(47) states it in operative words: in force 1 January 2025 unless one third objected before 1 October 2024.
retrieval_cards.why: The same machinery this paper's Q9 asks about in the abstract, here with a real instrument and real dates.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a trade facilitation convention reduce emissions?
retrieval_cards.answer: Through time, not through paper. Reliable standardised pre-arrival information makes just-in-time arrival possible: if the ship knows when the berth will actually be free she can reduce speed on passage rather than steaming hard to an anchorage and idling. Fuel consumption falls steeply with speed, so the same voyage with the same cargo burns materially less. Less congestion also means less machinery running at anchor for no transport work.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates answer 'less paper' and stop. The real argument is speed and fuel.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the limits of the benefit, and why does that matter to this question?
retrieval_cards.answer: The benefits are conditional. A single window that merely wraps the same paper documents in a web form delivers compliance and no benefit, and just-in-time arrival requires the charterparty to permit it - under a conventional laytime regime the ship is rewarded for arriving and tendering notice, not for arriving efficiently. The Convention removes the administrative obstacle; the commercial obstacle is untouched. It matters because the command verb is 'analyze', and an analysis that lists only advantages has not analysed anything.
retrieval_cards.why: Evaluation questions are marked on whether a reasoned, qualified conclusion actually appears.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business, and why is it needed?
retrieval_cards.answer: The harmonised reference data model for single window implementation, developed with the World Customs Organization, UN/CEFACT and ISO. It defines the data elements so that the same field means the same thing in every national system. Without it a single window would standardise the address but not the message, and the harmonisation the Convention requires would not be achieved.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the difference between electronic data and standardised data, which is the whole point of Standard 1.3quin.
