blocks.h: 1. The Convention and when it bit

blocks.p: The Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009 was adopted at a diplomatic conference in Hong Kong, China in May 2009 and entered into force on 26 June 2025 - more than fifteen years later. The delay is explained by Article 17, which imposes a triple condition: twenty-four months after not less than 15 States have consented to be bound, whose combined fleets are not less than 40 per cent of world gross tonnage, and whose combined maximum annual ship recycling volume over the preceding ten years is not less than 3 per cent of their combined tonnage - the third condition making the Convention impossible to bring into force without the major recycling States. At entry into force there were 24 Parties representing about 57 per cent of world tonnage, including Bangladesh, India, Pakistan and Turkiye.

ul: An Inventory of Hazardous Materials in three parts - materials in the structure and equipment, operationally generated wastes, and stores - with Parts II and III completed before recycling.
Survey and certification: an International Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and, after a final survey, an International Ready for Recycling Certificate.

Application to ships of 500 GT and above, except those operating throughout their life only in waters under the sovereignty or jurisdiction of the flag State (Article 3.3); existing ships must comply by 26 June 2030 or before going for recycling, whichever is earlier.
Control or prohibition of listed hazardous materials - asbestos, PCBs, ozone-depleting substances, and anti-fouling systems containing organotin compounds or cybutryne.
Recycling only at a facility authorised under the Convention in a Party State, working to a ship-specific Ship Recycling Plan, with notification of intent to recycle and a statement of completion.

blocks.h: 3. What it requires of recycling facilities

blocks.p: An IMO instrument normally regulates ships; this one reaches ashore and regulates the yard.

ul: Authorisation by the competent authority of the State, evidenced by a Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling.
A Ship Recycling Facility Plan covering worker safety and training, emergency preparedness and response, and the management of hazardous materials.
Safe-for-entry and safe-for-hot-work conditions to be established and maintained.
Controlled downstream management of the wastes removed - which is where the real burden falls.

India is one of the world's principal ship-recycling States, centred on the Alang-Sosiya yards in Gujarat, and it acceded on 28 November 2019, the Director General of Shipping depositing the instrument at the thirty-first IMO Assembly. That accession was decisive: it took the count to the required fifteen States and contributed heavily to the recycling-volume condition.

Domestically the Convention is given effect by the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 and the Recycling of Ships Rules, 2019, which anticipated entry into force by six years and apply Convention standards to ships recycled in India.
The maritime administration is the competent authority, authorising yards and approving ship recycling plans.

Indian ship recycling is governed by its own statute, not by the general merchant shipping legislation. The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 is separate legislation with its own machinery, and the general statute standing alongside it at this examination is the Merchant Shipping Act 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had received the assent of the President on 18 August 2025, three months before this paper, but assent is not commencement and it was not yet in force; it does not govern anything at this sitting. Either way the 2019 Act stands on its own feet.

Legitimacy and access to better tonnage. Owners who avoided South Asian yards on reputational grounds can now send ships to an authorised Indian facility with a defensible answer, which should raise both volume and quality of tonnage.
A level playing field. Competing recycling States must now meet the same standard, so the money India's yards spent upgrading ahead of entry into force is rewarded rather than punished on price.

Worker safety and environmental gain. Enforceable safe-for-hot-work and safe-for-entry requirements, training, protective equipment and controlled waste handling address the fatality and contamination record that has defined the industry's reputation.
Downstream industry and investment. Formalisation supports the steel re-rolling and second-hand equipment trades, and certification makes yards financeable and contractable on longer terms.

blocks.h: 6. How it stands to be impacted, and the balance

ul: Cost of compliance. Impermeable floors, containment, lifting equipment, and hazardous waste storage and treatment are capital-intensive. Small operators may not afford them, so the industry consolidates and some yards close.

Downstream waste capacity is the binding constraint. The Convention's obligations do not end at the yard gate, and treatment and disposal capacity for asbestos and other hazardous waste must exist for compliance to be real rather than documentary.

Price and leakage. Higher costs mean a lower price per light displacement tonne, creating an incentive to recycle elsewhere - including through a change of flag before the last voyage to a State outside the Convention.

Convention compliance is not European acceptance. The Convention does not expressly prohibit beaching, whereas the EU Ship Recycling Regulation maintains its own list of approved facilities on stricter terms. An Indian yard may be fully Convention-compliant and still not be EU-listed.

Enforcement is the credibility test. Authorisation has to be inspected and enforced; the industry remains under close external scrutiny, and a documentary-only regime would forfeit the reputational gain that is the main prize.

On balance, entry into force is net positive for India: it converts an early and expensive investment into a competitive advantage and legitimises the industry. The gain is conditional on downstream waste infrastructure and real enforcement keeping pace with certification - without them, the cost is incurred and the reputational benefit is not.

blocks.p: Three tasks are set inside one running stem, and candidates routinely answer only the first. Budget the paper deliberately: roughly a third on the Convention, and two thirds on India, split between benefit and impact. The word "or" in "benefit or be impacted" is not offering you a choice - it is asking for both sides and a judgement. An answer that only lists advantages has not done what was asked. Finish with an explicit balance; the archetype here is evaluation, and evaluation questions are marked on whether a reasoned conclusion actually appears.

blocks.h: The feature that makes this Convention different

blocks.p: Almost every IMO instrument regulates the ship - its construction, equipment, certificates and crew. The Hong Kong Convention is one of the very few that reaches ashore and regulates a facility on land, requiring the yard itself to be authorised, planned and inspected. That is why it took so long to bring into force: it needed the consent of States whose domestic industry, not merely whose fleet, would be regulated. And it is why Article 17's third condition exists - a recycling-volume threshold that made it impossible to bring the Convention into force over the objections of the recycling States. Read that way, India's accession in 2019 is not a footnote; it is one of the two or three events that made the Convention real.

blocks.h: The distinction that separates a good answer from a very good one

blocks.p: The Convention does not ban beaching. It requires safe and environmentally sound recycling, authorisation, planning and control - but it does not prescribe the method by which a ship is brought ashore. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation takes a stricter line and maintains its own list of approved facilities, which is why the acceptability of the Alang yards to European owners has been contested for years and is not settled by entry into force. So the accurate proposition is: Convention compliance is necessary for legitimacy but is not sufficient for European acceptance. A candidate who writes that the Convention has ended beaching, or that compliance automatically opens the EU market, has overstated it in exactly the way the examiner is watching for.

ul: Saying the Convention bans beaching, or that it makes Indian yards automatically acceptable to EU owners.
Giving the adoption year as the operative date. Adopted 2009, in force 26 June 2025 - the gap is the interesting part.
Reciting only the ship-side obligations and omitting the facility obligations, which are half the Convention.
Confusing the ICIHM (held through service life) with the Ready for Recycling Certificate (issued after the final survey, immediately before recycling).
Answering only the benefits when the question says benefit or be impacted, and giving no concluding judgement.

Attributing India's recycling law to the Merchant Shipping Act of any year. It is the separate Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 - and at this sitting the general Act is the 1958 one, the 2025 Act having been assented but not commenced.
Quoting a percentage share of world recycling. The figures vary widely between sources; name Alang-Sosiya instead.

blocks.p:
"Which Indian statute governs ship recycling, and which general Act stands alongside it?" The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 with the Rules of 2019, and at this examination the general statute is the Merchant Shipping Act 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had been passed and had received assent on 18 August 2025 - three months before this paper - but had not commenced, and an Act that has not commenced is not law. It was brought into force on 15 March 2026. Naming the 2025 Act as the governing statute here is the single most attractive wrong answer available, precisely because it is the newest thing a candidate will have read about. When it did commence, its repeal provision s.324(1) reached only the 1958 Act and the Coasting Vessels Act 1838, so the 2019 Act would have been untouched in any event.

"Why did it take sixteen years?" Article 17's three conditions, and specifically the recycling-volume threshold, which required the recycling States themselves to join.

"Your ship is going for recycling next month. Which certificate?" The International Ready for Recycling Certificate, issued after the final survey, with Parts II and III of the inventory completed.

"By when must an existing ship have an inventory?" 26 June 2030, or before going for recycling, whichever comes first.

ul: When was the Convention adopted and when did it enter into force? Adopted May 2009; in force 26 June 2025.
What are the three entry-into-force conditions? Fifteen States, forty per cent of world gross tonnage, and three per cent combined annual recycling volume - then twenty-four months.
When did India accede? 28 November 2019, deposited by the Director General of Shipping at the thirty-first IMO Assembly.
Which Indian statute implements it? The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019, with the Recycling of Ships Rules, 2019.
What are the three parts of the Inventory of Hazardous Materials? Materials in the structure and equipment; operationally generated wastes; and stores.
What must a recycling yard hold? A Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling, and a Ship Recycling Facility Plan.
Does the Convention prohibit beaching? No. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation applies a stricter standard through its own list of approved facilities.

blocks.p: SHIP - SHORE - INDIA - SCALES. Ship: inventory, certificates, 500 gross tonnage, 2030 (steps 1 to 2). Shore: authorisation, facility plan, safe for entry and hot work, downstream waste (step 3). India: acceded 2019, Recycling of Ships Act 2019, competent authority, untouched by the 2025 Act (step 4). Scales: weigh benefit against impact and land a judgement (steps 5 to 6). For the dates alone: adopted 2009, India acceded 2019, in force 2025, existing ships by 2030 - a decade apart each time, which makes the sequence easy to hold.

The statutory position is also strong, because the Gazette text of the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 and the commencement notification S.O. 1244(E) were both read directly for QP2607 Q7: Act No. 24 of 2025, assent 18 August 2025, commencement 15 March 2026. blocks.h: The one line to check in any older worked answer

blocks.p: This topic has a hard boundary running through it, and it falls before this examination rather than after it. Until 26 June 2025 the Hong Kong Convention had been adopted but was not in force, so the honest answer was that it was still awaiting its Article 17 conditions - with no entry-into-force date to give, no Party count, no tonnage figure and no operative obligations on ships or yards to describe. By this sitting it had been in force for five months, and every one of those things can and must be stated. If you are revising from notes or a worked answer prepared before mid-2025, that is the first line to check, because the change is not a detail - it converts the whole answer from a description of what a convention would require into a description of what it does require. It is also the reason the Party count and tonnage in this answer are given expressly as the position at entry into force: accessions have continued since, and a figure quoted without that qualification goes stale the moment another State joins.

blocks.h: This paper asks the same thing twice, from two directions

blocks.p: Q9 of this same paper asks about the procedure for entry into force of an IMO convention, and specifically about the conditions observed for a convention of important technical nature. This Convention is the live worked example, and it is a better one than SOLAS because its condition was actually satisfied only five months before you sat down. Article 17 is a triple condition, not the usual double one: 24 months after 15 States, 40 per cent of world gross tonnage, and 3 per cent combined maximum annual recycling volume. The third limb is the whole story - it made the Convention impossible to bring into force without the consent of the States whose own industry would be regulated, which is why India's accession in 2019 was decisive and why the whole thing took sixteen years. Answer either question and you have most of the other.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Hong Kong Convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the Convention and when it bit. 2 what it requires of ships. 3 what it requires of recycling facilities. 4 India's position and implementing law. 5 how India benefits. 6 how it is impacted, and the balance.
retrieval_cards.why: A third on the Convention, two thirds on India - and a stated judgement at the end.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the Hong Kong Convention's key dates.
retrieval_cards.answer: Adopted at Hong Kong, China in May 2009. Entered into force 26 June 2025. India acceded 28 November 2019. Existing ships must hold an inventory by 26 June 2030, or before going for recycling, whichever is earlier.
retrieval_cards.why: Four dates roughly a decade apart - easy to hold as a sequence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the Article 17 entry-into-force conditions?
retrieval_cards.answer: Twenty-four months after not less than 15 States have consented to be bound, whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 40 per cent of world gross tonnage, and whose combined maximum annual ship recycling volume over the preceding ten years is not less than 3 per cent of their combined tonnage.
retrieval_cards.why: The third condition is what made the recycling States indispensable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the Hong Kong Convention prohibit beaching, and does compliance open the EU market?
retrieval_cards.answer: No to both. The Convention requires safe and environmentally sound recycling, authorisation and planning, but does not prescribe how a ship is brought ashore. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation applies a stricter standard through its own list of approved facilities, so a fully compliant Indian yard may still not be EU-listed.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most overstated proposition in this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statutes govern ship recycling and general merchant shipping at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ship recycling is governed by the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 and the Recycling of Ships Rules, 2019 - separate legislation with its own machinery. The general merchant shipping statute at this examination is the Merchant Shipping Act 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had received assent on 18 August 2025 but had not commenced and was not law at this sitting; it came into force on 15 March 2026, and even then its s.324(1) repealed only the 1958 Act and the Coasting Vessels Act 1838, leaving the 2019 Act untouched.
retrieval_cards.why: Assent is not commencement, and this paper falls squarely in the gap between the two.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the ICIHM from the Ready for Recycling Certificate.
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials is held through the ship's service life, following initial and renewal surveys. The International Ready for Recycling Certificate is issued after the final survey, immediately before recycling, once Parts II and III of the inventory are completed and the ship recycling plan is in place.
retrieval_cards.why: One runs for the ship's life; the other is issued once, at the end.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a ship recycling facility hold under the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling issued by the competent authority, and a Ship Recycling Facility Plan covering worker safety and training, emergency preparedness and response, and management of hazardous materials, with safe-for-entry and safe-for-hot-work conditions maintained.
retrieval_cards.why: The facility obligations are half the Convention and are routinely omitted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the binding constraint on real compliance in India?
retrieval_cards.answer: Downstream waste treatment and disposal capacity. The Convention's obligations do not end at the yard gate, and without treatment capacity for asbestos and other hazardous waste, compliance becomes documentary rather than real - which would forfeit the reputational gain that is the main prize.
retrieval_cards.why: The sharpest point available in the evaluation limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian instruments implement the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 and the Recycling of Ships Rules, 2019, enacted six years before the Convention entered into force. The maritime administration is the competent authority, authorising yards and approving ship recycling plans.
retrieval_cards.why: India legislated ahead of entry into force, which is part of the significance.

questions.understand_first: Ship recycling is where two hard truths meet. An old ship contains materials nobody would allow aboard a new one, and the countries that do the work most cheaply are the least equipped to absorb the harm of doing it badly. The Convention's answer is to make the ship carry her own disclosure: a list of what hazardous material is actually built into her, kept current throughout her life, so that the yard which finally cuts her up knows what it is cutting into before it starts. The other half of the scheme binds the yard - authorised facilities, a specific plan for each ship, and a controlled place to do the work. For India this is not a foreign imposition; it is the direction the better yards were already travelling, given legal force. That is what converts the cost into an advantage, because a yard that has already upgraded now has something its unregulated competitors cannot offer. The impact falls hardest on the smaller plots that cannot fund the upgrade.

sources: PRIMARY (via MIW verification record QP2508/Q7, from QP2602/Q7): IMO conventions page - the treaty process. Adoption is by the relevant IMO organ or by a diplomatic conference. A State may express consent by signature alone where the treaty so provides; most multilateral treaties instead allow signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, where signature does not bind and the State must subsequently deposit a formal instrument with the depositary. The practice originated when communications were slow, protecting representatives from exceeding their authority, and States now use it to allow time to enact the necessary domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements. It cites Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties Article 14(2) for acceptance and approval and Article 15 for accession.

PRIMARY (via MIW verification record QP2508/Q7, from QP2602/Q7): IMO conventions page - entry into force and amendment. A convention becomes binding only after governments formally accept it. Early conventions typically required acceptance by two-thirds of contracting States. Conventions of an important technical nature generally set higher requirements involving both a number of States and a percentage of world merchant fleet gross tonnage. The tacit acceptance procedure was devised to accelerate amendment: an amendment is deemed to have been accepted unless objections are received before a deadline. Amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never received enough acceptances under the explicit procedure and none entered into force.

PRIMARY (READ IN FULL THIS SESSION): Resolution FAL.15(47), adopted 17 March 2023, Amendments to the Annex to the Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic, 1965, read from the IMO resolutions CDN. Operative paragraph 1 adopts the amendments in accordance with article VII(2)(a). Operative paragraph 2 DETERMINES, in accordance with article VII(2)(b), that the amendments shall enter into force on 1 January 2025 unless, prior to 1 October 2024, at least one third of Contracting Governments have notified the Secretary-General in writing that they do not accept the amendments. This is the tacit acceptance procedure stated in operative text, with both dates, and it is the same procedure this question asks about.

PRIMARY (via MIW verification record QP2508/Q7): IMO Circular Letter No.5005, 11 April 2025. The Secretary-General transmits the draft revised consolidated MARPOL Annex VI 'in accordance with article 16(2)(a) of the MARPOL Convention ... for consideration with a view to adoption at MEPC/ES.2 (14 to 17 October 2025) in accordance with articles 16(2)(b), (c) and (d) of said Convention'. This establishes which limb of MARPOL article 16 governs circulation and which governs adoption.

PRIMARY (READ THIS SESSION): IMO press briefing on the outcome of MEPC/ES.2, 14 to 17 October 2025. The IMO Net-Zero Framework was NOT adopted. The extraordinary session was adjourned and will be reconvened in twelve months' time, that is in October 2026, Member States continuing to work towards consensus in the interim. The Intersessional Working Group on GHG emissions reduction proceeded as scheduled from 20 to 24 October 2025.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (via MIW verification record QP2508/Q7, from QP2602/Q7): convention summaries confirming the entry into force conditions actually used. SOLAS 1974 was adopted on 1 November 1974 and entered into force on 25 May 1980, its condition being acceptance by not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping. The 1978 MARPOL Protocol provided for entry into force twelve months after not less than fifteen States, the combined merchant fleets of which constitute not less than fifty per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping, had become Parties. For SOLAS 1974 an amendment to the technical annexes is deemed accepted at the end of two years from communication unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments or by Governments whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage.

blocks.h: 1. Adoption is not entry into force

blocks.p: A convention is adopted either by the competent IMO organ - the Assembly, MSC, MEPC or Legal Committee - or by a diplomatic conference. Adoption settles the text and does no more: it binds no State, and an adopted convention may never enter into force at all. The text is then opened for signature and deposited with the Secretary-General of IMO as depositary.

blocks.h: 2. How a State expresses consent to be bound

blocks.p: Between adoption and entry into force sits the step that actually matters: each State must express its consent to be bound, by one of three routes -

ul: signature alone, where the treaty so provides or the negotiating States so agreed;
signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, which is the normal course for multilateral conventions;
accession, where the State did not sign within the signature period.

blocks.p: In the second and third cases the State is bound only on depositing a formal instrument with the depositary, who records it, counts it towards the entry into force condition, and notifies all other States.

blocks.h: 3. The two terms the question names

blocks.p: (ii) Signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval. The State signs, but the signature does not bind it; it indicates an intention to proceed. The State becomes a party only on later depositing an instrument of ratification. Its modern purpose is to give the State time to enact the necessary domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements before committing internationally. Acceptance and approval are the same act under less formal names, used where a constitution does not demand the fuller procedure: VCLT Article 14(2) provides that consent is expressed by acceptance or approval under conditions similar to those which apply to ratification. In legal effect the three are identical.

(i) Accession. The means by which a State becomes party to a treaty it did not sign - because the signature period has closed, or because it was not a negotiating State. It is a single step: no prior signature, simply deposit of an instrument of accession, permitted by VCLT Article 15 where the treaty so provides. Once deposited it has exactly the same legal effect as ratification. The difference is the route, not the destination.

blocks.h: 4. The entry into force provision, and why it matters

blocks.p: Every convention contains a final clause fixing entry into force, normally a threshold of acceptances plus a waiting period. Its importance is fourfold:

ul: it prevents an instrument binding a handful of States while the rest operate to another standard, which would distort competition;
it fixes a certain date from which obligations, surveys and certificates run, so Administrations, recognised organisations, owners and yards all work to one deadline;
it provides the interval in which flag States legislate, class develops rules, and industry builds or retrofits;
it gives legitimacy - a convention in force across most world tonnage can be enforced through port State control against ships of non-parties, which is what makes no more favourable treatment work.

blocks.h: 5. Conventions of an important technical nature

blocks.p: For a convention of important technical nature - one dictating construction, equipment or operation - States observe a stiffer double condition: a number of States and a percentage of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping. A count of States alone could be satisfied by many small registries while the major fleets stayed outside, leaving a convention in force on paper and irrelevant at sea.

ul: SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, requiring not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping; in force 25 May 1980.
The 1978 MARPOL Protocol - in force twelve months after not less than fifteen States constituting not less than fifty per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage had become Parties.

blocks.p: Older conventions typically required two-thirds of contracting States, which occasionally meant more acceptances were needed to bring an instrument into force than to amend it.

This paper supplies its own worked example, and it is a good one because the condition was actually satisfied only months before this examination. The Hong Kong Convention uses a triple condition under Article 17 - 24 months after ratification by 15 States, representing 40 per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage, whose combined maximum annual ship recycling volume over the preceding ten years is not less than 3 per cent of their combined tonnage. The third limb is what made it so slow: it required the major recycling States to join, not merely the major fleet States. It entered into force on 26 June 2025.

blocks.h: 6. Keeping the convention current once in force

blocks.p: A technical convention is worthless if it cannot keep pace, and explicit acceptance failed on exactly that point: amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never received enough acceptances and none entered into force.

IMO's answer was the tacit acceptance procedure, used in SOLAS 1974, MARPOL, the FAL Convention and the collision regulations. It reverses the default: an amendment to the technical annexes is deemed accepted on a specified date unless objections are received beforehand from an agreed number of Parties. For SOLAS 1974 an amendment is deemed accepted at the end of two years from communication to Contracting Governments, unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments, or by Governments whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage. Amendments now enter into force typically within 18 to 24 months.

The procedure can be quoted exactly, from an instrument that took effect earlier in the year of this examination. Resolution FAL.15(47), adopted 17 March 2023 under FAL Convention article VII(2)(a), determines under article VII(2)(b) that the amendments shall enter into force on 1 January 2025 unless, prior to 1 October 2024, at least one third of Contracting Governments have notified the Secretary-General in writing that they do not accept them. No such objection was made and the amendments took effect on 1 January 2025. That is tacit acceptance in operative words, with both of its dates.

It is worth ending on the point the question begins with, because a case running at the date of this examination proves it. Under MARPOL article 16(2)(a) the Secretary-General circulated the draft revised Annex VI - the IMO Net-Zero Framework - on 11 April 2025, expressly for consideration with a view to adoption at an extraordinary session under article 16(2)(b), (c) and (d). That session, MEPC/ES.2, met from 14 to 17 October 2025 - one month before this paper - and adjourned for twelve months without adopting the Framework. Circulation had occurred; the adoption step had been convened and not taken. A candidate who understands this question can say precisely why that instrument bound nobody at the date of the examination.

Finally, once a convention is in force internationally each flag State must still give it domestic effect. In India at this examination that is the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the rules made under it, and it is that domestic instrument which is enforced against the ship.

The route answers them in the order asked and gives the two named terms a heading of their own, because the examiner has singled them out and an answer that defines them in passing inside a general narrative will not be credited for them. Steps 6 and 7 are the pay-off: a candidate who can name tacit acceptance, quote a real determination with its dates, and then point to an adoption that did not happen has shown he understands the machinery rather than memorised it.

blocks.h: Four words that are not synonyms

blocks.p: Adoption settles the text. Signature may or may not bind, depending on what the treaty says. Ratification, acceptance, approval or accession is the act that binds the State, and it binds on deposit, not on decision at home. Entry into force is when the instrument starts to operate, for those States and thereafter for later parties. Candidates use all four as though they meant the same thing, and the whole question is built on their not meaning the same thing.

blocks.h: This paper answers its own question three times over

blocks.p: Revise this question together with two others on the same paper, because between them they supply every stage of the ladder as a real case. The Hong Kong Convention shows an entry into force condition satisfied - a triple condition, met after sixteen years, in force from 26 June 2025. The FAL amendments show tacit acceptance completed - determined in 2023, unopposed, effective 1 January 2025. And the Net-Zero Framework shows an adoption step convened and not taken, one month before this examination. Abstract machinery in the morning; three live cases on the same question paper.

blocks.h: The same problem exists in domestic law

blocks.p: An Indian Act is passed, then receives assent, then commences on a date appointed by notification - and it is not law until it commences. That is structurally the same three-stage problem as adoption, ratification and entry into force. The example current at this examination is exact: the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had received the assent of the President on 18 August 2025, three months before this paper, and had not commenced. It was brought into force only on 15 March 2026. At this sitting the operative statute was still the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 - and a candidate who wrote that the 2025 Act governed would have been wrong for exactly the reason this question is about.

blocks.h: Why tonnage and not just a headcount

blocks.p: The double condition looks like bureaucratic detail and is in fact the most commercially significant sentence in the answer. A safety convention that binds fifty small registries and none of the major fleets creates a competitive distortion rather than a safety improvement: compliant ships carry the cost and non-compliant ships take the trade. Requiring a percentage of world gross tonnage ensures the instrument binds the fleet that actually carries the cargo, which is what then makes port State control and no more favourable treatment effective against the remainder. The Hong Kong Convention goes one better and requires a percentage of world recycling capacity too, because a ship recycling convention that the recycling States had not joined would have regulated nothing.

Treating accession as a lesser status. Once deposited it has identical effect to ratification.
Saying ratification is deposit with IMO of a signed convention. It is deposit of a separate formal instrument.
Giving the entry into force condition as a number of States only, and omitting the tonnage percentage, on a question that expressly asks about conventions of important technical nature.
Describing tacit acceptance as automatic amendment. It is deemed acceptance in the absence of objection by a specified proportion.
Stopping at entry into force and never mentioning that the flag State must still give domestic effect - which is what actually binds the ship.
'State the provision and its importance' - two demands. Describing the provision without saying why it matters loses half of them.

A currency trap in reverse: the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 is easy to reach for as the domestic instrument, and at this examination it had received assent but had not commenced. The answer is the 1958 Act.

questions.understand_first: The point of this question is that a convention passes through several distinct stages, and at every stage it is not yet law for your ship. Adoption fixes the words. Signature usually promises nothing. Ratification or accession binds the State, and only when the instrument is physically deposited. Entry into force starts the obligations running. And even then, what is actually enforced against the ship in an Indian port is the domestic legislation giving effect to the convention. A Chief Engineer who can place an instrument on that ladder can answer 'does this apply to me?' - which is what the question is really about. This paper is unusually generous to anyone who has understood it, because it carries three live cases of the ladder at three different rungs: a condition satisfied, an amendment tacitly accepted, and an adoption convened and not taken.
